speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN SPEAKER'S GALLERY OF FRENCH DELEGATES TO MEETING OF CANADA-FRANCE INTERPARLIAMENTARY ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
I have the honour to bring to the attention of hon. members the presence in the Speaker's Gallery of the French delegation to the annual meeting of the France-Canada Inter-Parliamentary Association. The National Assembly of France has again shown the importance it attributes to the Association by the eminence of its delegates to this year's meeting. I particularly want to note the presence of the head of the delegation, Mr. Lucien Neuwirth, hon. member for the Loire department, Questor of the National Assembly and Secretary-General of our Association.
Mr. Neuwirth and the other members of the delegation come to Canada and to Parliament not only as parliamentary colleagues but also as friends. On behalf of this House, I extend a most cordial welcome to these gentlemen.

maintopic: MOTIONS TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 YOUTH   ALLEGED MISHANDLING OF FUNDS IN ADMINISTRATION OF OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM, TORONTO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the charges of mishandling of funds by the federal government in the administration of the Opportunities for Youth program in Toronto.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTIONS TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 YOUTH   ALLEGED MISHANDLING OF FUNDS IN ADMINISTRATION OF OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH PROGRAM, TORONTO
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has given the Chair notice of his intention to propose this motion under the terms of Standing Order 26. I might say that a similar intention had been indicated to the Chair by the hon. member for Egmont, but there was a slight difficulty in relation to the time of notice and it was agreed that perhaps the motion proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would apply equally to the motion indicated by the hon. member for Egmont.
The Chair has studied very closely the motion proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. With his knowledge of the rules, precedents and practice in reference to Standing Order 26, I believe he will appreciate that it would be very difficult for the Chair to accept the motion at the present time. It seems to me that this is the kind of proposal which should be put to the House by way of a substantive motion for consideration in due course, perhaps by the House itself or by a committee, rather than under the terms of Standing Order 26.
I might suggest that perhaps this is more of a proposal to be put to the House under the terms of Standing Order 43, as was done, rather than under Standing Order 26, but that is a question of judgment, I suppose, or even of taste. One hon. member might prefer to put it under Standing Order 26 and another under Standing Order 43. But I do not believe this is the kind of subject which can be considered by the House under the terms of Standing Order 26.
I must also suggest to hon. members that there is the possibility of debate on other occasions. In fact I have had the opportunity during the last few days on a similar

June 10, 1971

ruling to indicate that there will be many such opportunities during the days ahead to debate these matters. I would assume that hon. members would want to avail themselves of these opportunities to consider the very important matter raised by the hon. members for Egmont and Winnipeg North Centre.

speechtext:

military arms cache found in Great Britain and, if so, could the minister inform the House whether these arms had been sold to a foreign government or whether they had been disposed of to private individuals in Canada and subsequently resold?
Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of National
Defence): Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of the question. The Canadian representatives in London have sought to find out from the British authorities the details of the weapons in question referred to in the news story but up to the moment no information has been received. So far as I can determine from the Department of External Affairs, the Department of National Defence and the Department of Supply and Services, we have had no inquiries whatsoever from the British officials with respect to these weapons. With regard to possible disposal, I should indicate that there have been disposals of weapons in Europe by the Canadian Armed Forces in years past to the agencies of foreign governments but strictly on the condition that they were to be rendered into scrap. speechtext: When the House rose last evening it was considering motions Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5 in the name of the hon. member for Mackenzie. The hon. member for Mackenzie had the floor.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RATE PER BUSHEL, EMERGENCY PAYMENTS, EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO RYE, FLAXSEED AND RAPESEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night toward the end of my remarks I was commenting on the fact that the committee had been studying suggestions made by various farm organizations with regard to the bill now under consideration. I pointed out that these submissions were carefully considered by all committee members. I also volunteered the information that some of us in the opposition understood the submissions which were being made. It seems to me, however, that the government or the executive branch of the governmentthe minister, if he is to be singled out-has been frustrated either from within or without.
First of all, the minister has to respond to advice by civil servants that certain amendments are necessary for administrative purposes. I maintain that far too much consideration is given to making things comfortable for the administration and far too little for the people who are affected by the legislation we pass. Only second or third grade consideration is given to their convenience. This comment applies not only to the present bill but to every piece of legislation with which I am familiar. I do not say it happens 100 per cent of the time but it happens for far too much of the time, if I can speak from my own experience in this House. Too many things are done to make it easier for those in administrative positions who begin their work at eight o'clock and leave at five; during the summer, during the hot weather, they leave their offices at four o'clock because of the lack of air conditioning and the inconvenience of rush hour traffic. If you talk to a farmer along those lines, he will say: Hot days are best for killing wheat. Provided the tractor does not heat up he is out there working. In this case, only one side of the question is being considered. The government is in a hurry to get its money. It is determined to get it, and the devil take the consequences.
The attitude of the government has to change in favour of people. If we are to serve the people effectively and look after their requirements, the committee system must function more effectively than it is at present. There were great hopes for the new committee system when it was created by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). To some extent we went into it with enthusiasm regardless of the fact that it overloaded hon. members in many cases and regardless of the fact that certain work was being done in other committees to which we would have liked to dedicate ourselves. In terms of committee membership, we tried to concentrate on people who were particularly interested in the subject matter, people who were better informed, if you wish. Being more informed, I was willing to suggest that the government supporters should vote at that particular stage for two amendments I had presented and they accepted one. I thought that the consideration given by the committee would be far more valid than any consideration the House might have given, that is to say, if the committee system is to have any value at all. It was the Liberal whip who appointed government members to the committee and the committee was comprised of members who know something about the subject. The committee decided that in the interests of improving the legislation that this particular amendment should be accepted.
Reversing such a decision made by the committee is an indication that the government has no confidence in its own members on the committee. In view of the flippant attitude taken to the committee I suggest that perhaps the whole system of committees should be disbanded and that we should forget about committees studying legislation. The only thing left to the government is to take authority unto itself by executive order and to state that

June 10, 1971

since legislation is presented by civil servants the government feels it is adequate as such and about any representations that might be made thereon are irrelevant, that people who know something about the subject need not be heard, that any amendments that might be made would be useless, that any opposition in this House of Commons is unwarranted, that any member who dares speak in opposition to the government is wasting his time, and that it is unnecessary to have any elections.
This goes to the heart of what I suspect, and have suspected for some time, we have as a government in this country. This government has gone farther than any of us dared think in its haste to outrun the NDP and their philosophy and the communist philosophy. I do not know whether they are more scared of the NDP than they are of themselves. Let the government listen to some of the criticism that comes from within, because it is more valid now than ever before.
It is becoming more and more difficult to preserve democratic institutions in the western world than ever before simply because pressures against them are mounting. If the committee system has now been changed to the point where its considerations do mean something, then let some of the amendments moved in committee be accepted. Let them not be rejected on the basis that they were moved by members who do not support the government. I have been a member of the House for 13 years and have sat on various committees, interesting myself in many of them. But I feel we have now reached the point where the minister tells his own supporters what amendments to accept and what not to accept. In turn the minister gets his directions from the man sitting beside him, either the deputy minister or the assistant deputy minister.
This is not democracy, Mr. Speaker. What we are now witnessing is an attempt to reverse a decision made by elected Members of Parliament which, if successful, will be a slap in the face for all Canadians and for democracy. If the government values democracy at all, then let it reject the present committee system or else accept amendments made in committee. Simply to say that the fact that my amendment is moved by a member of the opposition makes it invalid is no argument at all. To say the least, I feel very frustrated, as dedicated as I may be to any particular bill under study. Many members of the House on both sides are dedicated, and they too find they are being frustrated because they are given instructions from above.
These members are highly regarded in their communities and many of them were elected to this House because they were experienced men. They are now being told by the minister or by a civil servant that they know nothing about the matters they are considering. I would suggest to the minister that regardless of what value a man places upon himself no man is so all-knowing that the combined opinions of people knowledgeable about a certain matter are of no consequence. For example, industrial conditions are constantly changing, and so that we can change at the same time we have to make amendments. You cannot view the subject from one side alone.
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act
The other day the committee accepted very readily an amendment that I moved. In the afternoon I moved another amendment that I suggest was identical to the previous one. But somewhere along the line the members of the Liberal caucus must have held a conference and said to themselves: "Look, we cannot accept too many amendments from the opposition; otherwise it will be an opposition bill and we cannot have that. We must not give the opposition any more credit than we dare, so we must throw the other amendments out." As a result, my amendment was defeated.
What recourse do I have, Mr. Speaker? All I can do is bring the matter to the House and record it for posterity in the hope that those who read my speech or listen to my words will understand the futility of the whole system. This government, which wants to promote itself and itself alone, is dedicated to only one thing. The government thinks it can get more co-operation from its civil servants by following their line. I suggest that in the interests of building a better country the government had better listen to opposition members. I do not expect, and neither does any other member of the House, opposition amendments to be accepted 100 per cent, but the proposition that an opposition amendment must be rejected because the ideas of the mover are all wrong is absolutely unacceptable today. We do represent an area. As a matter of fact the opposition members in the Conservative party represent a far larger rural area than members of the Liberal party ever did. To suggest at this time that the government has absolute knowledge of the requirements is wrong. It follows logically that somewhere along the line it must listen to somebody.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in respect of the amendments put forward by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Kor-chinski) regarding Bill C-239. The four amendments deal at length with the principles to be followed by applicants or farmers taking out cash advances, how they must repay and whether or not an interest charge will be levied against the advance.
It is interesting to note what the minister had to say in reference to the third amendment proposed by the hon. member for Mackenzie. This is to be found at page 61 of committee proceedings No. 53. He said:
[DOT]	3 Tan ,has this money, is not delivering grain, and then is found to be m default, he should pay interest on the whole penod that he had the use of the money, because that is in effect converting it to what he did, which is using it as a loan instead of an advance. And I urge this very strongly upon you.
That is what the minister stated and it is perfectly clear what he is trying to do is narrow the scope of cash advance legislation in order to save the government as much money as possible. We heard in the committee that cash advance legislation, being interest free, in essence cost the federal government in the neighbourhood of $3

June 10, 1971
Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act million. It is quite clear that the main object of this bill is to narrow cash advance legislation and apply interest on part of the advance. The amount of cash advances the government will provide interest free will be reduced. This is the whole theme of this legislation and it fits a pattern this government is following right along in respect of agricultural legislation.
The government has withdrawn all the financial assistance it can withdraw effectively. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has reduced bonuses for hogs, for land and for wool. He has repeatedly made reductions. The present minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, and I say that because the way the Saskatchewan election is going he may not be in charge very long, has given some indication in Bill C-244, the grain stabilization program, that he intends to withdraw money the government committed itself to in the past. Apparently it will not make this commitment in the future. It is regrettable that all this legislation should be concentrated toward this one objective or goal.
The hon. member's amendments are very pertinent because on many occasions a farmer will take out a cash advance on grain he has on hand for delivery. Let us take last winter or the present time as an example. The price of barley selling at the Lakehead is in the neighbourhood of $1.17. For some reason there is a 12 cent charge per bushel on grain from the Crowfoot area delivered at the Lakehead. That brings the price down to $1.05 per bushel. Again for some unknown reason, when the farmer delivers his grain he receives between 71 and 73 cents per bushel. The farmers wonder what happens to this other 30 cents. Will they receive it in their final payments or is it absorbed by storage costs? Where does it go?
A farmer might want a cash advance on his barley. He is faced with a difficult decision. He must ask himself whether to deliver it to the elevator and accept 72 cents per bushel or sell it to a feed mill or feed lot down the road at 80 cents per bushel in cash. Suppose the farmer takes a cash advance on his grain in storage under this legislation and sells it to the elevator. After doing so the price on the market at the feed mill or feed lot goes up over 80 cents per bushel, much more than he would receive by delivering it to the elevator, and he sells it to the feed lot. He might fully have intended when he took out the cash advance to repay it with the barley. He has a difficult decision whether to sell to the feed lot and pay interest on his cash advance from the time he received it, or deliver it to the elevator.
Even the interest rate he will have to pay is not spelled out. The minister said that the rate would be announced at the beginning of every crop year. I suppose that is better than nothing. In most cases cash advances will be taken out in the fall of the previous year, so the farmer would be taking the advance without knowing the exact interest rate he might have to pay. The minister shakes his head in a negative fashion; he can correct me if I am wrong, but that is the meaning of his remarks as I understood them.
To date many cash advances have been taken out and repaid with cash. I forget the exact figure but I think the minister stated that something like 15,000 or 16,000 advances were repaid partially in cash. The minister has stated that if the cash portion amounts to more than $500 the farmer will have to pay interest on the total cash advance. If it is less than $500 no action will be taken and he will not have to pay interest.
In any case the amendment moved by the hon. member for Mackenzie clearly states that the interest on a cash advance taken out on grain should apply only to that grain, and there should be no retroactive action by the government which would in fact penalize the farmer because he made a shrewd decision to sell the grain to another commercial outlet at a higher rate.
I can see a great deal of merit in the four amendments now before the House and for that reason I commend them to hon. members.

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING RATE PER BUSHEL, EMERGENCY PAYMENTS, EXTENSION OF APPLICATION TO RYE, FLAXSEED AND RAPESEED

Mr. Speaker, I should like to reply in part to the point raised by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr, Horner). The interest rate for a crop year will be set prior to the crop year and any default which occurs in connection with an advance, no matter how much later it occurs, will be related to the interest rate for that crop year. So the farmer taking an advance will know his position exactly.
The first amendment of this group really follows a decision taken earlier in the House in favour of an amendment which stood in my name. Amendment No. 3 is difficult in that it would be technically impossible in terms of no interest being payable at all even if no delivery at all was made, because there would be no point or date from which the interest rate could be set.
The point in this-and this applies as well as to amendment No. 5-is that these interest rates are payable only in relation to loans which are in default; that is to say, where the person has undertaken to deliver grain when quotas are available and has failed in that undertaking, has had notice from the board to do so and has still failed in the undertaking. It is only then that interest is payable and it seems perfectly reasonable that it should date from the time of the loan and not from any particular later time.
The technical difficulties with amendment No. 3 include the fact that a person who attempts to misuse the system could avoid an interest payment simply by delivering a single bushel of grain. The technical wording would absolve him from the interest claim. It is important to keep the system of cash advances working well. It is respected; it is well received. Abuses where persons take a loan and never intend to keep their undertaking only bring the program into disrepute. The very great majority of farmers use the system well. They use it when they need the money. They do not even take an advance if they can avoid it. For them we should try to keep the system working as well as possible. This is the point of the original form of the bill.

They say that a choice of whether to be involved or not has been offered to one level of government. Now, let me read from the brief which the federation drew up under date of May 12.
We request that local authorities be given the same option as provincial authorities are given to cover either all or none ol their employees.
The municipalities argue strongly that their resources are already extremely strained as a result of fiscal and monetary policies, yet they are faced with extra costs consequent upon the inclusion under the terms of this clause of firemen, policemen and, in particular, of schoolteachers-some 250,000 of them. This would mean that the cities would incur an extra cost burden, one which is really related to an increased burden on the taxpayer. Moneys for government purposes, regardless of level, come from the same person. The hon. member for Battle River is seeking to impress upon the government that if this provision is enacted the taxpayer, who is already burdened by heavy taxation for municipal services, will be forced to pay additional taxes consequent upon the inclusion of employees of municipalities in the insurance scheme. You can never calculate the amount, but I do not think anyone would deny that there is an onerous responsibility on any individual now who is faced by taxation from all levels, in all ways and by all means.

And I apologize to him as profusely as I can, Mr. Speaker. Certainly, I would not want to confuse him with the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
I had started to say that I appreciated the concern of the hon. member for Hamilton West for the financial plight of the municipalities, but I suggest that this is a plight that should be dealt with in some more substantial and direct way. You do not solve this problem just by relieving the municipalities of the cost of paying unemployment insurance premiums; that problem calls for a recasting of the division of taxation revenues in this country among the federal, provincial and municipal levels.
The fact of the matter is that the aim of this bill is to make unemployment insurance coverage as universal as possible. I am in accord with that principle, and I think that any exceptions to it should be only those for which there is an unanswerable argument. As a matter of fact, there are some exceptions that I think should not be here; but as I understand it the reason that provinces are excepted is that there is a constitutional rule-maybe it is a myth but it is such a firmly rooted myth that it is practically the law-that the Crown cannot tax the Crown. In other words, the Crown in the right of Canada cannot pass a law to tax the Crown in the right of the provinces. I understand that is the reason the provincial authorities are excluded from compulsory coverage under the Unemployment Insurance Act, though in the next clause of the bill provision is made for the provinces to be included, if they so desire and thus indicate to the federal government.
No such inhibition obtains in the case of the municipalities. Therefore, I think we should keep the exclusions from unemployment insurance coverage to a minimum. We have to do it in the case of the provinces, but we do not have to do it in the case of the municipali-

June 10, 1971

ties. There are many thousands of employees who work for government at the municipal level, and their employment is subject to uncertainty as it is in many other areas of work. I think we would do the workers who are employed by municipal governments a service if we kept them under unemployment insurance coverage, and therefore I hope that my hon. friend will not press this amendment.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) put forward an argument that I have heard many times to the effect that somehow it is not fair for the taxpayer to pay for unemployment insurance premiums as if they were a tax. This argument has been raised by school teachers and others and I want to deal with it for a moment because, with all respect, it just does not make sense.
The fact is that every unemployment insurance premium is paid by the employer and the consumer. If as a consumer I buy goods, I know very well that I am paying for the premiums paid by employers. Certainly, I do not think the employers are for one moment making a gift. In reality, the same ratepayer or consumer pays for both insurance premiums. To put forward the argument that somehow this is an exceptional tax on municipal ratepayers just does not make sense. In addition, the purpose of unemployment insurance is to give a benefit to the employee. That really is the essential element. How can anyone justify the position that I, as an employee of a municipality, will not get the benefit of this legislation- which I say here and now is very meaningful legislation-while the employee of another corporation or private enterprise concern does get the benefit? How long does the hon. member for Hamilton West think that this situation will last? Public or municipal employees will immediately demand that there be an equivalent municipal fund from which they can draw. All you will have is a fragmentation of this scheme. With all respect, I cannot see the sense in this amendment.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have carefully listened to the arguments of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander).
I cannot accept them nor approve the motion as put since, to my knowledge, in my region-and I imagine it is so all across the country-municipalities hire workers temporarily, especially during the summer months and lay them off in the fall. If these workers are not protected by some social legislation, such as unemployment insurance, they will have to apply for welfare assistance should they be unable to find employment elsewhere.
Mr. Speaker, were the motion now being considered passed and enforced, the workers would be in a very bad predicament as is often the case in Quebec. A large number of temporary employees of the Public Works and Highway Departments, for instance, are not contributing to the unemployment insurance fund because they are prevented from doing so by the provincial authorities. These people are laid-off in the fall and if they are unable to find employment elsewhere, they have to rely 24107-651
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
on social welfare which has nothing left but crumbs to give them.
Hence, I think that even if the municipalities find it somewhat constlier, they should nevertheless be required to pay contributions to the unemployment insurance fund, together with their employees so that the latter may benefit from the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The unemployment insurance act is perfect, I know. In fact, I think that if we could have full employment, that would be much more effective.
But as we have to live in such a situation, we have to try and protect the greatest possible number of workers by this legislation, and I believe that municipal employees should be among those.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a word or two about this proposed amendment. I support it for a basic reason. I take strong objection to one level of government taking the attitude that it knows best and then proceeding to act as God in the conviction it is right and therefore knows what is best for everyone.
The municipalities of this country have a segment of jurisdiction wh.ch, in my judgment, should not be impaired by any other level of government. It is my belief that an option should be open to municipal governments to decide whether they want their employees under the Unemployment Insurance Act. If the act has all the merits, the government says it has, it is obvious what their choice will be. Nevertheless, it is not for us to say that some municipalities might prefer, under perhaps unique circumstances, to not have its employees covered by unemployment insurance and, therefore, as employers not have to pay a tax which is imposed by another level of government.
There should be a right to an option rather than an imposition on one level of government by another level of government. I know bureaucrats and perhaps socialists-I look to the people on my left and I hope they will excuse me for using that term-like to see everything standardized and shoved into neat, watertight compartments. They are everlastingly trying to put Canadian citizens and municipalities into a kind of Procrustean bed of their own choosing. If they are short they like to stretch them, if they are too long they like to chop pieces off. I think this is bad legislation from that point of view and, therefore, I heartily support the purpose of this amendment. It is not intended to cut off unemployment insurance from employees of municipalities who wish to be covered. Rather, it gives municiplaities the same option as the provinces.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself rather intrigued by the extraordinary kind of logic or lack of it displayed by my congenial friend the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean). While I am quite happy to have him refer to me as a socialist, I am not really rising to speak on this amendment as a social-

June 10, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
ist. I rise to speak on it as someone who attempts to have a practical interest in the welfare of the working people of this country, and to deal with a bill presented by a government which is certainly not prepared to call itself socialist.
This argument that the laws made by one level of government should not impinge in any way on the functions of another level seems to be extraordinary. If one were to follow that through, it would mean the people working for a municipality would be completely exempt from provincial legislation setting minimum wages. In fact, the muncipalities would be separate little feudal kingdoms within a kingdom. I think that if the hon. member would reflect upon this he would realize how absurd his logic is if it were brought to its ultimate conclusion.
I have listened to many arguments in this House, some of them advanced by political colleagues of the hon. member for Malpeque, regarding the matter of the federal government accepting its responsibility to pay municipal taxes on federal property lying within the boundaries of municipalities. This is a position I was prepared to support long before it became the accepted practice for the federal government to more or less automatically make a payment equivalent to and in lieu of taxes.
As far as I am concerned, I do not feel we should stand on these fine points of constitutional jurisdiction. Jurisdiction of each level of government should apply to its own field. I would be quite happy to see this strange constitutional fiction about municipalities not being able to tax the Crown on property just as it taxes any other property in municipalities done away with, but the hon. member for Malpeque and his colleagues, in putting forward this argument, are proceeding in a direction exactly opposite to that of the principle of equity of function among various levels of government.
I submit to the hon. member that despite his eloquent plea his argument is not well founded in principle, nor indeed is the amendment. I certainly would be much happier with the bill if this provision exempting the provinces were not included. I do not want to make an issue of it at this time, and obviously I cannot because I have not put down a report stage amendment in my name to that effect, but my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) did suggest that perhaps it was only fiction. Inasmuch as federal jurisdiction over unemployment insurance is embodied in the British North America Act, we might have been wiser simply to have said, all employers, either public or private, will be treated the same way under the same circumstances as far as the question of unemployment insurance is concerned.
Now, the amendment suggests we should move into the area of the municipal level. The question of the distinction which might be drawn between private employers and public or semi-public employers is one which has been discussed quite often. In the 1955 review of the Unemployment Insurance Act, the big debate in this area
was over the question of hospitals, and whether hospitals as employers should or should not be required to participate in the unemployment insurance scheme. So, I would suggest the amendment is a retrograde step. In some respects I believe the provision in the bill which exempts the provinces is a retrograde step, because if one ties that particular clause to the next clause it becomes apparent that many provincial employees across the country may be worse off than they are now. This is why I should like to say a word in favour of the principle at least of arriving at a point where neither municipalities nor provinces will be listed here as excepted employers.
Certainly, the employees of the government of British Columbia are concerned about the situation because with the provision of the exemption here and the provisions in the succeeding clauses, those who, at the option of the government of British Columbia, have long enjoyed the benefits of unemployment insurance coverage may suddenly be pulled out of a scheme which the minister and others have said is designed to move in the direction of greater universality. My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, may have smother word or two to say on that subject in respect of the next clause. However, in view of the line the debate is taking, I should like to indicate that far from supporting the approach in the amendment we are dealing with I believe we should delete that clause and remove the exemption for both provincial and municipal governments. I believe this suggestion is perhaps particularly apt because the government is taking the position that federal employees should be participants in the scheme. That puts a different complexion on the whole thing than that which existed at the time of the earlier major re-write of this legislation when the government did not take that position.
I hope that, as a result of this bill, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) and the commission will be able to convince the provincial governments of the logic of agreeing that all their employees must be covered on the same basis as private employers will be required to cover their employees.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to support this amendment because I believe it is in line with an option which is already available to the provincial legislatures. We heard in the committee that a province, if it so wished, could exempt its employees from the operation of this bill, presumably through the BNA Act. This amendment, I think, would simply tidy up the situation and allow the municipalities the same privilege. Until this privilege is taken away from the provinces then a certain amount of inequity will be created unless the municipalities are allowed the same privilege. We are dealing with provincial and municipal employees as well as groups of workers who are allied to municipal and provincial jurisdictions. These, in the main, are new workers who are to be taken into the plan. Out of one million odd extra people in the plan, I believe perhaps
400,000	come from these two groups as well as 250,000 from teachers, 400,000 from hospital workers and 50,000 from nurses, plus the armed forces and so on.

June 10, 1971

I should like to point out that teachers in some provinces are direct employees of the provincial government and in others fall under some sort of quasi-municipal jurisdiction. I believe the teachers, as a group, have strongly objected to inclusion in the unemployment insurance plan, believing the mechanism would be a means whereby if one province decided to carry its teachers this would mean that other areas would follow suit. The teachers point out that their unemployment will occur at the beginning of their careers before they have paid into the plan and that this will make it difficult for them to take advantage of the plan. Indeed, for the teaching profession it would seem these people would have to so organize their lives as to be unemployed in order to take advantage of the plan. If this amendment is adopted it will permit some uniformity in dealing with those teachers in provinces where there is a municipal authority involved.
There is a similar situation in respect of nurses- approximately 50,000-who are employed by municipal hospitals. Generally speaking, these are young people who have a high degree of mobility in their employment. There has been no significant unemployment in respect of nurses in the past 25 years. Indeed, we have scoured the globe to find registered nurses to fill our hospitals. This amendment would allow those nurses, who are municipal employees and who do not wish to be included in the unemployment insurance legislation, to be taken out. I think this would be a means of equalizing the application of the unemployment insurance payments or deductions until at least all provinces agree to participate. In any case, if the unemployment insurance legislation should prove to be so good, there would be a rush of people to be included and there would be no problem in enticing groups to enter.
This amendment would make the principle of universality more flexible and would decrease its application to some extent. I realize that the inclusion of one million workers who have little or no chance of being unemployed will make the statistics look good. I would make an exception in the case of certain hospital workers who, in my opinion, should come under unemployment insurance. There are workers in professions or trades which can make their demands felt, so that at the time of the next pay raise they will get sufficient take-home pay to make up for the deductions they may have lost. I believe it is a good idea that this amendment be adopted. I think it would remove some of the universality of application of this bill which I do not believe is in the best interests of the unemployment insurance principle which we all defend to the best of our ability.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking briefly to the amendment which has been proposed, I should like to indicate I am opposed to it. It would seem to me if we are to have a successful unemployment insurance plan, we must cover as many workers in Canada as possible. The amendment calls for the inclusion of municipalities in the opting-out provision, thus allowing them to exempt their employees from
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 making unemployment insurance payments. I think this is a foolish amendment. There are thousands of municipalities across Canada, some of them with two or three employees many of whom are only part time employees. Are we going to allow some of these small municipalities that might not have too much cash to say "we are going to save a few dollars by not allowing any of our casual employees to get stamps in their books for unemployment insurance benefits in the event they are out of work"? There is no doubt that some of the municipalities hire teachers, but out where I come from the schools do all the hiring. We are not too worried about the municipalities hiring teachers or nurses, but it seems to me to be very foolish to suggest that the thousands of municipalities from one end of Canada to the other be given the right to opt out of the unemployment insurance plan. We will not hesitate to vote the amendment down.
There is one more point which was raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) and which I, too, would like to draw to the attention of the minister. It deals with this very section. As I read the bill, it gives the right to the various provinces to be all in or all out. Perhaps I am misinterpreting the bill, but in British Columbia we have 6,000 civil service employees who are covered by the plan. They are casual employees, and the rest of the employees who are not covered are upset. They want to be under the plan. I suggest to the minister that he look at clause 4(e). All we have to do is move an amendment to insert the words "in whole or in part" in that clause. Let the provinces come into the plan in whole or in part. This is the way around the problem, and I suggest that the minister look at it in that context. If the province of British Columbia decided to opt out, there would be 6,000 casual employees who would then not be covered by the unemployment insurance plan and they could get into trouble. I do not think this should be our objective, and I suggest that we find some way of getting around this point.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I rise to support this amendment because, over the years, I have had considerable experience with school boards, having served as chairman of one for a good number of years and having, in that time, wrestled with school budgets. I do know something of the cost that will be added to the school budget if and when this program is put into force. We have talked about this from time to time. While the amendment refers to municipalities, let us not be under any illusion that the municipalities will supply the funds to the school boards who will be paying the employer share of the contributions. I should like to put on the record what this will cost approximately. I have a complete table for all the provinces in Canada. I do not wish to take the time of the House by reading it all, but I would like to cite what it will cost the province of Ontario and then to refer to the total cost.

June 10, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
In Ontario we have approximately 103,000 teachers. The average salary in Ontario is approximately $7,767. The teacher contribution per week would be roughly $1.19. This is based on teacher premiums over a four year period, and this table is based on the situation if this act were in full force today. The employers' share for these teachers would be $86.63 per teacher, making a total addition to the school budget in the province of Ontario of $8,922,890. Taken all across Canada, the total bill comes to $22,666,407. This is certainly not peanuts.
All across the country, and particularly in the province of Ontario, people are screaming their heads off about the high cost of education and the share which the municipalities must bear, which in many cases approximates 60 per cent of the municipal taxpayer's bill. So we are not talkmg about small amounts of money. For this reason alone, I think this amendment deserves the support of every member in the House if he is at all interested in what his local people are having to pay in municipal taxes. I could go on and talk about teachers being drawn into this plan unwillingly, unable and unlikely to benefit from it. The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) has already pointed out that the time when the teachers would most benefit from the plan would be the time when they had no equity in the plan, that is when they are at the beginning of their teaching careers. I could argue along that line, but the point I want to make as strongly as possible is the great increase in cost to the municipal taxpayer if this plan is implemented.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I have listened with a great deal of attention to the various members who have spoken about this proposed amendment. I must say at the very outset that I cannot support the amendment, nor can 1 suggest to the government benches that we should support it. Of course, members from some of the other parties have indicated the same. The whole concept of unemployment insurance is that we intend to make this plan as universal as possible.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there seems to be some uncertainty as to what word the minister used. I hope he said "other parties".

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, other major parties. All parties in the House are major. I am simply saying that all enlightened parties oppose the amendment. The point I want to make is that the basic concept that we have proposed, which was accepted by the House on second reading and accepted in the committee, is to make this plan as universal as possible in so far as employees in Canada are concerned.
Our relationship with the provinces has been such that at present, under the old act, the provinces have been permitted, as one hon. member just suggested, to be partly in and partly out. Of course, the consequence of this is that the only groups that have been covered by the provinces in the main have been, what you might call, seasonal workers. This has been unfair to the other people who have to finance the plan, the other employers and employees who do not have the same privilege. It is

insuring bad risks as opposed to good risks. One of the features of the existing plan is the option of the province to cover segments of workers. This option is being removed by saying, in effect, to the provinces that if they want coverage for their employees they should cover them all, not just those whom they think it is in their financial interest to cover.
I want to stray from the amendment which deals in particular with the municipalities and get on to the subject of teachers. Under this plan teachers are in, and if this provision is knocked out there will be no plan. We have been engaged in these discussions for several months. We have done all there is to be done to satisfy the teachers. The cost to the school boards has been analysed. I have met with representatives of school boards across this country. They are relatively satisfied, as are the teachers. While admittedly it is an added burden to the school boards to cover teachers, this is true of all employers in this country. However, the savings to the provinces, and therefore to the municipalities, under the Canada Assistance Plan more than offsets it. Because of the lower eligibility and higher premiums, for a period of 51 weeks we are covering people who would normally be forced to go on the welfare rolls of their municipalities. For instance, in so far as the province of Prince Edward Island is concerned the hon. member for Mal-peque (Mr. MacLean) may be interested to know that if we were to extend to the municipalities the same right as we have proposed in the bill for the provinces, over 60 per cent of the municipal employees in P.E.I. who are presently covered might not be.
I think the hon. member who spoke for the Social Credit party quite properly pointed out that many municipalities across the country do what they can for the casual workers, the less fortunate in the community, by providing work for them for six, seven, eight or nine months of the year. These people would be denied unemployment insurance while they were out of work. At present 79 per cent of the employees working for civic governments in Newfoundland are covered by unemployment insurance. The other 21 per cent could be workers in certain categories. They could be teachers working as civil servants, and also they could be employees earning over the $7,500 or $7,800 threshold. These figures run from approximately 30 per cent to 79 per cent, and so this amendment is contrary to the effect of some of the amendments that will be proposed by the same party later to other clauses of the bill.
This bill broadens the concept of universality. The party opposite cannot have it both ways. We stand for universality, and as has been pointed out it would be even more desirable if all the provinces were to fall in line like all other employers in the country. However, I am confident that when this bill is passed the overwhelming majority of the prov'nces will be glad to enter the plan. Frankly, it is inconceivable to me that any province would stay out, particularly in light of the figures I have quoted which show that the majority of civic employees will now be covered.
June 10, 1971

This amendment, if adopted, would tend to deny coverage to the municipal worker. The decision would not be made by the worker. It would be made by the civic authorities, by elected aldermen who in some communities may be people who have never known what it is to be out of work. Since they would be worrying about administrative costs they might autocratically, without consulting their employees, decide that municipalities should not be covered by the act.
I suggest that if adopted the amendment would weaken the act rather than strengthen it. It certainly flies completely in the face of the principle of universality which has been the cornerstone of the act. The desire and thrust of all the members of the committee, representing all parties, were directed to making the act as universal as possible, as later amendments will show, and so I would hope that this amendment is defeated.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lincoln M. Alexander (Hamilton West) moved:
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
That Bill C-229, an Act respecting unemployment insurance in Canada, be amended by adding next after subclause (1) of clause 4, following line 35 at page 5, the following:
"(2) The Commission may, with the approval of the Governor in Council and subject to affirmative resolution of Parliament, make regulations for including in insurable employment any business within the definition of "business" in the Income Tax Act."
He said: Mr. Speaker, the minister dealt with universality when speaking with respect to motion No. 2. Perhaps hon. members may think that I am now attempting to do a flip-flop, but having listened to the brilliance and eloquence of the minister's remarks on universality, I wish to give notice that I would like this motion amended. I can advise the House that the government is prepared to go along with this motion, subject to it being amended in such a way as to make it more acceptable to the government, and to strengthen the intent of what we are attempting to do. All that the motion attempts to do is give those in the category of self-employed persons the
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
opportunity of becoming involved in unemployment insurance. We are attempting to open a door whereby those who are sufficiently in need, even though they may be self-employed, can be covered by unemployment insurance.
I refer to certain significant parts of the motion. It reads "the Commission may-". That is a permissive word. Then, it continues, "with the approval of the Governor in Council and subject to affirmative resolution of Parliament, make regulations for including in insurable employment any business within the definition of "business' in the Income Tax Act." Certainly a lot of selfemployed people may not want to become involved with unemployment insurance, but on the other hand a lot of others may want coverage. I am appreciative of the government's helpfulness to the opposition in this respect, and I will be seeking unanimous consent to have four words included in the motion in order to bring it into an area of acceptability. In the fourth line of the motion after the word "any" I suggest that the following words be inserted "person employed in a" so that it would read "make regulations for including in insurable employment any person employed in a business within the definition of "business" in the Income Tax Act." I am grateful for the assistance of the government. I am sure that, as a result of this co-operation, this amendment in the long-run will be of some assistance to those who are presently excluded from the act. I also hope that hon. members to my left will see the reasoning behind the amendment and agree to support it.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to the amendment as reworded. What this simply reiterates is the power of the Unemployment Insurance Commission to define by regulation employers as employees for the sake of the act. The amendment just makes this a little more specific, giving the commission power to include for coverage at some later date, if necessary, certain groups of people. I think the act would be stronger as a result of this amendment and I am pleased to accept it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we certainly are prepared to give our support to the amendment to the motion. However, Mr. Speaker, I am a little puzzled that the hon. member has added these words because it seems to me he has departed from his desire to cover self-employed people. The hon. member says he does not think so, but this is a matter

June 10, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
that has to be ruled upon at some point. With these words in, it is now allowed to the commission to pass regulations which will include a person who is employed in a business which is defined as such in the Income Tax Act. It is still limited to an employed person, and does not cover a self-employed person. We accept this, but I still hope the day will come when a way will be found to include self-employed persons under the provisions of this act. We have spent a good deal of time on this in committee, and those of us who were there realized the complications and difficulties that exist but it is still a fact that there are many self-employed persons who lose their income just as much for reasons beyond their control as is the case with employed persons. After all, I have just alluded to the reason for unemployment insurance, namely, to provide for the continuation of income of persons who lose their income for reasons beyond their control. We think that should be applied across the board.
While I am on my feet, I will look the minister in the eye and he will know what I am about to get into at this point. Because we are talking about including other classes of people by means of regulation, I should like to suggest either that the act be amended or that the minister tell us that he will have it looked at under the provisions of this amendment, to deal with the question of covering Members of Parliament under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
This has been suggested a number of times, Mr. Speaker, and it has been taken up in two ways. Those of us who have proposed it have done so because we believe in the principle of universality. We think that, just as we are requiring other people to pay into the unemployment insurance fund, we should be required to pay into it ourselves. Other people have taken it in a different light, and indeed some newspapers have suggested that this was just a proposal to add to the many perquisites and benefits that flow from being a Member of Parliament. When we have debated the pensions, salaries and expense allowances of Members of Parliament, I think I have made it pretty clear that we have to exercise restraint. I have said very clearly that we have gone too far in these areas and, therefore, I do not think I can be accused of proposing to add more. I think that some people being brought under unemployment insurance coverage have a legitimate grievance when they say, "You are bringing us under it but you have not brought yourselves under it."

Mr. Speaker, I think I am on the fringes of being in order, but I think I can state the case in less time than it would take to prove that I am in order. I will simply say that I hope the minister at some point would get the consent of the
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) .1
House to extend the principle of universality, which is the aim of this motion, so that we will be included. I hope it will be done in such a way that we will not get the benefit of unemployment insurance if we go out on pension and so on, but I hope a way will be found to see that we carry our fair share by paying our premiums into the Unemployment Insurance Fund, as we ought to do.
If I may, I go back now and say that I think what I said was at least on the fringes of being in order. The purpose of this amendment is to extend the principle of universality and I should like to see that extension include Members of Parliament.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.

If I might, I should like to take advantage of the invitation of the hon. member who is on the fringe of being in order, therefore I am on the same fringe. In view of the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), and in view of the possibility which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has raised that the objective of the hon. member has not been reached by the additional words, I wonder if 1 would be in order in suggesting to the House that this section stand. In that way, I would have an opportunity to speak with the legal officers of the department in order that we may, through the proper wording, obtain what the hon. member for Hamilton West has suggested. Possibly at the same time, we could have it worded in such a manner that in the future, through regulation the Unemployment Insurance Commission, when it is deemed appropriate, could include such groups of people as Members of Parliament. If the time is appropriate, and if after study we find that we can convince people that the thing will not be abusive, perhaps the clause can be worded in such a way that the pension benefits of retiring Members of Parliament and things of this nature are taken into consideration in conjunction with the benefits of unemployment insurance for those Members of Parliament who might not be returning next year.
Possibly I would be able to do both those things with a reworded subamendment. Mr. Speaker, after consulting a little later in the day with the officials of the department. Before the supper hour, we could perhaps come back and clear up that particular clause.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us one of the most important amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. This amendment deals with the waiting period, that is the period of t me to establish one's rights to benefits. Under the present Unemployment Insurance Act, the waiting peiiod is one week. The government proposes to extend this waiting period to two weeks. My amendment proposes that this should not be done and that it should remain as at present with a one week waiting period. I shall try to put forth my arguments why the waiting period should remain as at present.
This is an insurance bill. An insurance bill is always drafted to provide insurance and protection. When one is entitled to protection or insurance, he wants it right away. He does not want to wait for two or three weeks or even one week. This is the case in such insurance plans as accident and sickness, life insurance or automobile accident. Indeed, if you are involved in an automobile accident, an adjuster is on the job almost immediately. Fire insurance operates in the same way. With other forms of insurance, the adjustment or claim is attended to immediately. The government is now asking these persons to wait one week longer for their unemployment insurance benefits.
Under our present economic situation in Canada, we have a very high rate of unemployment. Welfare costs average as high as 68 per cent. Indeed, in the city of Toronto last year, welfare costs were $45 million. If people must wait an extra week for the'r unemployment insurance, I am convinced there will be only one result. More people will have to go on welfare to tide them over until the'r unemployment insurance cheque arrives.
I am sure all hon. members realize that there are thousands and thousands of people who live from week to week. The amount of their Friday n'ght cheque is already committed before they receive it. It is required for rent or they go shopping on Saturday for food and clothing for the children. When a person becomes unemployed, he needs this unemployment insurance cheque immediately. He cannot be expected to wait a week longer than he is now waiting.
I am sure all hon. members have had experience with situations in which something has happened to unemployment insurance benefit cheques. Either the computer went haywire or the form was improperly filled out. As a result of persons not receiving their benefit cheques, they get in touch with their Member of Parliament to see what they should do. They have no money on hand and there is no food in the house. The money is due to them but they have not received it. What do we expect them to do? How are they going to feed their children? The government is now going to ask them to wait an additional week before receiving this benefit. I am convinced that this will increase the welfare costs in this country.
If we are putting forward an insurance bill, we must provide proper insurance. I know the minister will say that this suggestion will cost more money and by extend-
6578

June 10, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 ing the waiting period another week the government will save approximately $160 million. This does not interest the unemployed. They are interested in proper coverage and an immediate settlement of their claims. I know the point will be raised that the premium will be reduced from $1.40 to 77 cents. Why drop it down to that level? Why not strike a half way mark and still provide the one-week waiting period rather than the two-week waiting period?
I am sure that every member in this House has received many letters and telegrams from many organizations and people pleading for the government not to include this extra waiting period in this new plan. I received a telegram from one union, Local 541 U.E. It reads in part:
We have grave concern about the increased waiting period, the possibility of reduced benefits for many of the unemployed

There is grave concern about this extra waiting period among those people who are covered by unemployment insurance schemes. The added welfare costs to which I have referred will have to be borne by the municipalities. It is the taxpayers who will have to pay for this. The unemployment insurance scheme is contributed to by the employer and the employee, and the cost of administration is paid by the federal government. If people are going to be forced to accept welfare because of the added waiting period, the employer and employee, particularly the employer will have to pay in two ways, through his municipal taxes and through unemployment insurance. I plead with the minister and his officials to give this amendment very serious consideration.
Another argument that might be made by the minister is that the benefits are going to be higher under the new plan. The unemployed person is not as concerned about this as about having the benefit available immediately. He says "I need it now; I do not need it in the future, I need it when I am unemployed. That is today." As I said before, the waiting period is being extended to two weeks. Even with a one-week waiting period, from the time the form is filled out until the cheque arrives takes two or three weeks. By extending the waiting period to two weeks, it will be three weeks before he receives payment under this new unemployment insurance bill.
This is the most important change in this new bill. I hope the minister will give it a second thought. If the minister cannot see his way clear to accepting this amendment in its present form, I plead with him to give serious consideration to leaving the one-week waiting period the way it now is until such time as he gets the new bill into operation and gets the administrative problems ironed out. Goodness knows, the administration of this new bill will be a Midsummer Night's Dream for the officials concerned. They will be so busy ironing out the wrinkles in this new bill that it would be a great relief to them I am sure if the waiting period were left at one week, as it is now. Possibly the two-week waiting period could be introduced later on.
If the minister does not wish to do this, I will offer an alternative. Why does he not tie the waiting period in

with the national average unemployment figure? In other parts of the bill we find that the period of benefit entitlement is related to the national unemployment figure. If the national average is 4 per cent, the period will be ten weeks; if it is 5 per cent it will be 14 weeks, and so on. Why cannot the waiting period also be tied in on a similar basis? The length of the waiting period is an important part of the bill. I have therefore no hesitation in recommending motion No. 5 for the consideration of the House.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
At this time we are considering four proposed amendments, Nos. 4, 5, 7 and 8. Two of them are on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) and two of them in the name of my colleague from Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). Although their wording may vary slightly, they seek precisely the same thing. They seek to amend clauses 16 and 23 so that the waiting period under the new Unemployment Insurance Act will be one week, as it was under the old act, iiistead of two weeks as is now proposed by the government.
The workers of Canada have felt for a long time that the Unemployment Insurance Act is their legislation. They have become very familiar with its provisions and with its details. If I might speak particularly for the organized workers, I would say they have studied this legislation very thoroughly. Naturally, there are a number of provisions in the new bill which are of concern to the workers who have considered it, but I must say this point is one which seems to have provoked the widest misgivings, namely, the extension of the waiting period from one week to two weeks. The hon. member who has just spoken has called attention to some of the difficulties which will arise if this is done. I would like to underline what he said and to express the hope that the government will yet consider the request we are making in this respect.
The minister and his officials have been quite forthright with us in giving us the reasons for proposing this increase in the length of the waiting period. They have stated that it is their desire to improve the benefits available to unemployed workers and to reduce the premiums. More people are to be covered, benefits are at a higher rate, benefits are to be extended in the sense that sickness and maternity are to be covered, and so on. And the minister and his officials have made it clear to us that if Parliament is to provide these things, things which provide more money, funds have to be found in some way. So, they are to be found by bringing into the scheme people who have not been participants up to this point, and by cutting some benefits here and there. Here we are considering one of the benefits which is to be cut, namely, the right to draw unemployment insurance after a waiting period of only one week.
It has been my experience that workers, particularly the organized workers with whom I have had some connection, have never objected to any extra cost which would be involved in extending unemployment insurance benefits. I remember years ago when we first started arguing for coverage in times of illness that the question
June 10, 1971

was put in committees of the House of Commons to workers' representatives: Are you prepared to pay an extra premium if necessary for this extra benefit? The answer was always a ready and unqualified yes. I believe that is the story now. I believe that if we give the workers the right to a shorter waiting period, in other words, to begin collecting benefits in the second week rather than in the third week, they would be prepared to agree to contribute to the higher cost incurred.
As the bill stands, the amount of premium to be paid by the employee and the employer is to be fixed annually. Rates will be determined each fall for the ensuing calendar year, based on what the experience has been. No amendment to the monetary part of the bill is, therefore, required for the kind of amendment we are proposing. The extra cost to the workers as well as to the employers will be automatic. It is, of course, a fact, that the workers have been used to the one week waiting period. But one must make the point even more strongly that at times such as these when there is so much unemployment, when so many people have to live on a hand to mouth basis, it is not very acceptable to tell someone he should be willing to accept a waiting period of two weeks instead of one week because the benefits he is eventually to receive will be somewhat greater. I do not think we need take the time to argue it. This is one change on which we in the opposition parties are united. It is our hope that the government will agree to these motions when the vote is called. It would be even better if it were not necessary to vote, if the minister, who has already shown he is ready to agree to some changes, would tell us now that he will agree to this one.
In any case, I make it quite clear that we in this party support the necessary amendments to the act to provide that we keep in effect the one week waiting period rather than moving to the two weeks waiting period, which would be extremely difficult for those in this country who become unemployed.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to support the four amendments that are now being studied together, to the effect that the waiting period before receiving unemployment insurance benefits be one week instead of two weeks as set out in the bill.
Mr. Speaker, I support those amendments because as the mover pointed out a few minutes ago, by the time the worker receives unemployment insurance benefits his income has already been reduced and if he has to wait one more week-two weeks instead of one-he is being penalized, his income is further reduced.
As the hon. minister and others who took part in the debate on this bill pointed out, our aim here should be that the worker who is laid off should not be deprived of his income and have to face financial difficulties in supporting his family.
Mr. Speaker, I think the worker is not responsible for losing his job. He has nothing to do with that, as it is due to uncontrollable circumstances.
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
Therefore, I do not believe we should penalize more than is necessary the worker deprived of his job, by having him lose two weeks of unemployment insurance benefits instead of one.
I think that the current one-week waiting period is amply sufficient for anybody who lost his job to determine whether he can find another one. If he cannot succeed within one week I doubt he would in two.
Mr. Speaker, in the centre column of page 17 of the white paper on unemployment insurance, introduced a few months ago, you can read and I quote:
The traditional stability of occupations such as nursing, teaching, police work, the armed forces and the public service can no longer be taken for granted. Supply may become greater than demand; austerity measures can cause redundancy;
Everyone knows to what extent the government used restraint measures in its administration to fight inflation, for example, and each time restrictive measures have been adopted for one reason or another, the worker has always suffered from it. Because of the current administration and its predecessors, workers have been sufficiently penalized and should not be even more penalized.
I am confident that the minister and the other cabinet members will understand the arguments put forward and the reasons why the movers have suggested reducing the waiting period to one week. I wonder why anyone would try to extend the waiting period to two weeks.
I strongly support the movers and I hope that the government will consider this motion favourably as it did the first one at the very beginning of this debate.

speechtext:
The hon. member says "hear, hear". The point is that I am rarely accused of being very conservative-and that is quite a feeling-in my approach to social legislation that affects the workers. However, when we sat down to formulate this proposed change and many other fundamental changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act for the first time we took, perhaps, a global picture of how best to help the work force of this country at reasonable cost to employee as well as to employer.

June 10, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
While the workers of this country have, with some degree of justification, looked upon the Unemployment Insurance Act as their own, we all know that the cost of the plan since 1940 or 1942 when it came into existence has been borne not only by employees but also in equal amount by employers. The plan, therefore, is not the same as the one in the United States which is financed entirely and exclusively by employees; our plan is equally financed by the employers of Canada.
The hon. member has already alluded to the cost factors of many of the features of the plan. For example, the cost to the plan of reducing the two week waiting period to one week, as suggested, and which the workers claim they would be quite pleased to pay for, would run to about $160 million for the normal features of the plan. In addition, of course, you would have to meet the cost of the sickness and accident benefits which would come into effect after one week instead of two, which would mean that the cost would go up to somewhere around $300 million to $400 million.
If you try to apportion that amount of money into weekly contributions, this would run from a minimum of 65 cents a week to up to $2 a week for every employee and employer in this country, an astronomical figure. So, although this proposal may be desirable, it just is not realistic at this stage.
As I said in the committee, since it is the intention of the government, and presumably of subsequent governments, to review the Unemployment Insurance Act with much more frequency, it is quite possible that over the next three, four or five years, after we have had an opportunity to assess-
