speechtext:
I apologize, Mr. Speaker. I did not really realize how all-embracing that word is.
I was saying, however, that to reduce the two-week waiting period to a one-week waiting period would cost
$160 million minimum and could run perhaps as high as $400 million, depending upon the effect of the inclusion of the sickness and maternity features of the bill. So, although it may be desirable one day to get down to a zero waiting period, it is not practical or realistic now.
The second problem we have results from the introduction for the first time of these features in the unemployment insurance, that is, the extension to include people under unemployment insurance as a result of sickness or maternity. Quite frankly we need the two-week waiting period to make certain that people drawing unemployment for these particular reasons are in fact eligible. The administration period is bound to be greater with these new features than was previously the case when we did not have unemployment insurance benefits extended to cover sickness and maternity.
Hon. members are certainly very knowledgeable about the operation and know that the two weeks in many cases could mean eight days. People who register under the plan on Friday could become eligible in as little as eight days. So, the two-week period is highly desirable from an administrative point of view. For that very reason we want, and will make certain, that the unemployment insurance extended to those workers who are off because of illness or maternity is applied properly. Every effort will be made to make sure this is not intentionally or unintentionally abused. From an administrative point of view, we need those two weeks. As I mentioned, this could be as little as eight days or as much as 14 days, depending on when an individual applies and how long it takes to process the application. There are certain functions I do not want to get into in detail.
In addition, it might create a situation where such an individual would receive more money by staying at home than by working, so it would pay an individual to stay on unemployment insurance. We do not want to introduce intentionally any such disincentive. For those two reasons; the fact that the reduction in the waiting period from two weeks to one week would cost anywhere from $160 million a year and up, and the employees of the country would be glad to absorb it, and the fact that we need the time for administration purposes, we feel we cannot accept the amendment.
Such a reduction in time would place an equal burden on the employers of the country who, in the main, have been very responsive to our plan. These employers have advanced a minimum of objection to the features of the plan and generally find the bill very desirable. I suggest when the next review of the act takes place, three, four or five years hence, this could be one area of discussion, whether we can make an improvement by reducing the waiting period to one week. We will then have had five years' administrative experience in operating the plan. We would be able to anticipate the cost of the plan with even greater precision.
Although it is politically attractive to me, as the Minister of Labour, to recommend the acceptance of such an amendment, I must resist the temptation. As desirable as this amendment may be from a humanitarian point of

June 10, 1971

view and as a step in the direction toward an Utopian plan, we must look at what we have tried to do with this. We have tried to construct it in such a way that the workers in this country will get maximum benefits at a reasonable cost. We think we have been able to do this, which you will see it you look at it in the total picture rather than at segments of it. If we were to reduce the two-week period to one week we would substantially increase the weekly contribution, not only to employees at 65 cents a week minimum, but by a dollar or more a week to employers, or conversely we might reduce the benefits and thus reduce the pay-outs.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) quite honestly and properly suggested that the two-week period represents a savings to the plan. It also provides something equally as important. It provides an opportunity to administer the plan with a maximum degree of efficiency. These two things have made it possible for us to introduce maximum benefits with the smallest possible burden on the working force. While the principle of the amendment is socially desirable, I think it is premature, and in a sense this will be the main area on which amendments to the act in five years' time might centre.
Let me say in conclusion that we have to make certain the new features of the act in relation to sickness and maternity are administered properly. We need this time to check out many aspects of eligibility. This would be very difficult with a one-week waiting period. And I point out again that if an applicant registers on Friday this will mean really only eight days required to process a claim properly and ascertain whether the sickness is in reality a real sickness. We must check other aspects in respect of maternity as well.
Equally as important is the fact that the reduction from two weeks to one week would place an added financial burden on the plan amounting to $160 million to $400 million depending on the use of the sickness and maternity features. Even though employees might be quite happy to share the load in this regard, it would cost an extra 65 cents or a dollar a week. Furthermore, it might well interfere with sickness plans now in existence, some paid for by employers who provide some form of payment during a period of sickness. For all these reasons, I would respectfully ask the House to reject the amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the amendment before the House. I listened with a great deal of interest to the statement just made by the minister. He gave us the additional cost involved in cutting down the waiting period to one week. I must say I still do not accept the argument put forward. It seems to me if we are going to save between $160 million and $400 million in cost that sum of money still has to come from somewhere. It has to come out of the pockets of the workers, and these are the people receiving benefits from the sickness and maternity features, but these are workers without jobs. They can ill afford to lose this benefit because of the additional costs,
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
even though it will be spread nation-wide among these unemployed.
There is another point which I do not think was covered. If it was I must have missed it. The act as it now exists provides for a one-week waiting period in a benefit year of 52 weeks. The proposed legislation calls for a two-week period. The question I ask is what happens to those workers who have a series of jobs during the summer? They will not only lose two weeks but perhaps four weeks in a year, or maybe more. This waiting period is not going to be just a one-shot affair, at least as I read and understand the bill. If an individual is unemployed twice during the year, he will have a full month during which he will receive no unemployment insurance at all. There are a lot of people in this category. A very large number of casual workers in every part of Canada do not have just one job but a series of jobs. They lose considerable benefits, as I see it, unless the minister has more information on this. Is there to be more than one two-week waiting period in a year? They should be able to continue receiving benefit without interruption if they have sufficient stamps. I would like an explanation on this.
Some of the groups which have been writing to me are as worried about this aspect of the legislation as I am. I feel we should have left the one week stipulation in the regulations. I would have reversed the condition the minister has given this House. I think we should have tried this legislation for the first year or perhaps for the first two years. The government certainly will not be paying nearly as much in unemployment insurance costs as it paid under the old plan. As I read it, they will not be paying part of the cost of running the plan until there is over 4 per cent unemployment. Why do we not experiment for a year and let the government pick up the tab so that we might find out what it is to be, and then have a review at the end of the first or second year. This would be the proper approach.
Let us give the unemployed people in Canada a break. Let us tell them this is really a new plan. This is what it should be. This is the object of the legislation. There are some substantial improvements in the legislation, but this is one of the particularly weak sections of it. I still feel the amendment to cut back the waiting period to one week, as presently exists under the old plan, is a sound one which ought to be accepted by the minister.

speechtext:
Well, we have quality here which is extremely important. We do not need quantity. I have always been particularly concerned, and in fact I would say perturbed, about what would happen in respect of this particular clause. If I recall correctly, the present act indicates that those who will be entitled to unemployment benefits must have had an attachment to the labour force for 30 weeks in the past 104 weeks, with eight weeks being in the last year. When I think of that, I recall that our party has indicated not only in this House but also across the nation that we beg the minister not only to increase the benefits but also reduce the period of eligibility. I do not think anyone would attack us in that regard, particularly because of the cost of living these days, but I shall not go into that because we are not talking about the maximum benefit. I hope when we asked that the eligibility period be reduced the minister did not think we wished to give away things on a platter. When I look at the eight-week period it would seem to be a considerable change, in my humble opinion. The explanation I heard would lead me to believe that it was just a question of judgment whether it would be 6 weeks, 8 weeks, 10 weeks or 12 weeks.
I became increasingly concerned when I found that an eight-week attachment-if I recall correctly and if all things are equal-would allow one to receive 44 weeks of benefit. This is really what I would call a good thing. Surely, we are all in the position where we think about helping one another and being our brother's keeper. Certainly the government must at times, according to my philosophy, help people to help themselves. I wonder, however, whether in fact we are really helping people to help themselves when we reduce the eligibility period to eight weeks. I know I have been misquoted in the newspapers. I have been misunderstood as a result of these misquotations from not only the newspapers but also the radio. I have been quoted as saying the Canadian people are lazy. I have never said any such thing and do not
intend to say it. I realize I said that if I were involved I would be tempted to work for eight weeks only with the expectation of receiving 44 weeks of benefit, but certainly it would seem to me that when you hold out some inducement to a person all you are doing is trying to influence people to have little personal initiative in an effort to get ahead.
This is what concerns me and this is the reason I object most strenuously. I know the minister and his officials have indicated to me how important they feel this change is. For the life of me, however, I cannot understand it, particularly when in the committee we were given the impression that the eight-week period was just taken out of the air and was a question of judgment. When I look up at my friends, the officials sitting in the gallery, I wonder why their judgment did not allow them to pick 12 weeks, which I would think would be more in keeping with allowing a person to have initiative. If we are trying to follow the new line of thinking, which is to the effect that governments must be involved with people, it would seem to me we should try to leave people with a will to continue to work and make it on their own. How can we do that when we indicate to a person that all he has to do now is become attached to the labour force for eight weeks in a year and, if all goes well, he will be allowed 44 weeks of benefits. He might be earning $100 a week. Let us put it at $150 a week for eight weeks, and with the new benefits which he will be able to obtain, it appears to me that a person can acquire 44 times $100, which is $4,400.
Of course, the other important point is that it is taxable. Many people will understand that these benefits are not free. The minister indicated, rightly so, that we are going to give some benefits, but we will get something back from them. If you make $150 a week during the eight weeks you contribute, it seems to me that if things go well eventually you can take out $4,400. Perhaps I am wrong. I hope that the minister will clear that up, but as I understand it and as the officials have stated, that is the gist of it.
I could go on and on with it, but I just want to register my dismay and my lack of understanding of how the government can possibly think that this is an incentive. I thought that when we talked about unemployment insurance we meant temporary income maintenance. But 44 weeks is not temporary, it is permanent; as a matter of fact, it is a whole year's salary. I am not saying it is the best of salaries, but I am wondering what we are attempting to do. This is supposed to be temporary income maintenance to facilitate re-absorption into the productive activity of the work force.
All I can say in conclusion is that I am dismayed by this particular clause, and I am afraid that with all the good intentions the government may have, this clause is open to abuse. It removes the incentive that we are all seeking. It certainly does not enhance personal initiative. So, my two motions are an attempt to make the act more reasonable. What we are trying to do is to allow people

June 10, 1971

to help themselves. I think this is what the government should be doing.
The philosophy of my party is that the government should not move in until it is actually and really required. In other words, the individual should be able to help himself, and this is what I like about our philosophy. Governments should not just look after people from their birth to their death, but we are starting to move in this direction. Whether or not Canadian people can afford this is questionable. But I hope that the minister, as well as my colleagues in the House, will appreciate what I am saying. It is not that the Canadian people are lazy. Heavens, no, I would never say that. What I am saying is that when you hold out these enticements, these inducements, these carrots, there is bound to be abuse. I hope that the administration which will be set up will be able to cope with these abuses effectively, because I can foresee problems for the department and for the minister. What he has done, in effect, has been to remove the initiative from people to continue to seek work.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was very pleasant when we were debating the last set of amendments to be associated with the members of both of the other opposition parties. On that occasion we were unanimous. That unanimity is at this moment shattered by the stupidity of the motion that my friend has put down. I cannot say I am surprised in the sense that I am taken unawares because it is an amendment which my friends in the official opposition moved when we were in committee, but I thought it had been sufficiently dealt with there so that they would not be so foolish as to raise it again on the floor of the House.
I must say also that I find it quite inconsistent for my good friends to the right to want to improve unemployment insurance for the workers by cutting the waiting period from two weeks to one in the last debate and now wanting to make the whole scheme less attractive for the workers by making it necessary for them to have a longer attachment to the work force before they can collect benefits.
I also find it a piece of inconsistency for hon. members to my right to say that one of the things that is wrong- and this was said today-about bringing teachers under the plan is that the plan will not provide them with benefits when they need them, namely before they start to work at all. So in that instance they are really asking for no attachment. They were asking for benefits to be paid to certain people before they start to work, and now when the act proposes that they shall receive benefits after a period of eight weeks, they say, oh no, that is too soon, that is offering a carrot; it is a contribution to laziness, so we must make it 12 weeks.
I really think that the argument which my good friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), put up in which he builds a case of people paying this small unemployment insurance premium for eight weeks and then automatically collecting benefits, as he says, for 44 weeks, is a poor one. Although he did not put the actual multiplication in cold language, he gave the impression that they would receive $4,400 for a few weeks contribu-
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
tion, namely eight weeks contribution to the unemployment insurance fund. It does not work out that way.
Surely he knows that there are two kinds of claims, a minor claim and a major claim, and surely he knows that eight weeks does not entitle you to the full benefit. There are other conditions to be met. Surely, he also knows that you do not get a benefit of $100 a week unless you have had a certain period of employment at $150 a week. This kind of attack on the unemployment insurance scheme is all right when you read it in some of the Tory newspapers in the country, the financial papers and others.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about this amendment because I had trouble following the arguments of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander).
As the previous speaker, I am surprised to note the difference of opinions about his two motions. The hon. member for Hamilton West suggests that the period of employment entitling to unemployment insurance benefits should be raised from eight as mentioned in the bill, to 12 weeks.
Mr. Speaker, I think that this period of eight weeks is acceptable. I did not have the opportunity to check all the clauses of the bill but I understand that this eight-week period will exclude the clauses of the legislation

June 10, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 providing for a period of benefits during the slack season. I believe this is so. In my opinion, if we extended this period to 12 weeks, as the hon. member for Hamilton West requests, we would have to bring in other changes to the law or leave as it is the present provision concerning the seasonal period.
In my opinion, it would be preferable to approve the proposal in the bill providing for an employment period of eight weeks only.
There is another point that was not mentioned in this debate. In the remarks on the white paper on unemployment insurance, the students' problem has quite often been referred to. For instance, someone asked what the white paper on unemployment insurance provided for students. Obviously, a youth who has just completed his studies is very seldom credited with contributions to unemployment insurance. But with this short qualifying employment period of eight weeks it will happen often enough that during the holiday period students will have been able to work for these eight weeks, even during a single vacation, and so will have accumulated enough contributions to be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits when their course is completed if they do not find immediate employment.
Thanks to these eight weeks of employment accumulated during the preceding vacation, students will be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. If this period is extended to 12 weeks, they will be in difficulty.
This is why, Mr. Speaker, I must oppose the motion moved by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander).

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) sort of ridiculed the members of this party because we had fought for this amendment in the committee and had been beaten. He said the matter had been threshed over and therefore we should not discuss it again. If we follow that line of thinking, it means that once a member has lost any motion in this House he should never return to it, but I point out that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has fought for the same motion year after year in this House-

speechtext:
It must have been stupid because the House has always turned it down. When a member is beaten in committee, that does not prevent him from presenting his argument to the House. Therefore, I have no hesitation on speaking on this motion. The same hon. member talked about this party being inconsistent. Mr. Speaker, if we appear to be inconsistent, it is only because the bill is so full of inconsistencies that one cannot talk about it without appearing to be inconsistent.
The minister has said that the basis of the bill is universality. Throughout the committee hearings members of this party pointed out instances where the government had departed from the principle of universality.
But I must admit that the minister, with a display of co-operative spirit, has granted us some of the things we sought. The bill makes provision for a certain attachment to the labour force. It refers to increasing benefits because people need more money due to the higher cost of living. There is also a reference to extending benefits to people who do not have a long attachment to the labour force. But on the other hand, the government says that we must lengthen the waiting period otherwise the provisions of the bill will cost too much money. Just how can you talk consistently on a bill which contains so many inconsistent principles? This is a most illogical and inconsistent piece of legislation.
I was one of the members in committee who spoke about the qualifying period. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) asked the officials to tell him the basis for the eight weeks qualifying period, and in reply they gave what in hockey is known as a judgment call. In other words, they decided that eight weeks was a nice sounding figure. My hon. friend was told that this was the same as in the present act. I do not agree with that. It is true that under the act a person must have eight weeks attachment in the current year, but there is a stimulation that he must have a bit more than that going back over 104 weeks. We asked the officials why it should not be ten weeks, 12 weeks or 14 weeks, and the answer was that if it were extended to ten weeks it would exclude many people from the benefits given by the act. I attended many of the committee hearings and I did not hear any logical explanation from anyone with respect to the eight week figure. Why couldn't it be ten weeks or 12 weeks? That is the question we want answered. If we had asked the officials why not reduce it to two weeks, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would probably have said, hurrah. If the theory behind this legislation is that it is to look after all the people who are out of work, then why not reduce the period still further?
I do not want to be misquoted, as the hon. member for Hamilton West was, but I do want to express my belief that all the people who are out of work through no fault of their own should be looked after, but not all through the Unemployment Insurance Act. We have other general legislation. We have welfare legislation. Why destroy the whole intent of the Unemployment Insurance Act by extending much needed welfare through it to people who are out of work but who are not really in the labour force? When I say "not really in the labour force" I would like to give one or two examples of what reducing the work period to eight weeks can do. Take the example of a seasonally employed housewife, of a woman working in a department store at Christmas time. Her husband may be making $10,000 or $20,000 a year and not be in need of any assistance. If this clause is passed as it stands, the woman may work for eight weeks and draw benefits for 44 weeks. I am not going to quibble with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre about whether this is $100 a week; to me the important thing is that by working for eight weeks she can draw benefits for 44 weeks.

June 10, 1971

I took this up with an official one day in committee because I thought I must be on the wrong track and I could not believe the answer he gave me. I asked, "As a matter of law, if a person works eight weeks a year, he can draw benefits for the other 44 weeks?" He said, "That's right". So then I asked, "Can a person go back to work for eight weeks the next year and draw benefits for another 44 weeks?" He said, "That's right". I cannot find the logic in this provision or understand how it can be called insurance or how such a person can conceivably be classed as a worker.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, according to the hon. member, a person may work for only eight weeks each year and receive unemployment insurance benefits during 44 weeks. Could he tell us what would happen to the worker who lost his job through his own fault at the end of eight weeks?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT, 1971 PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION BENEFITS. PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I cannot answer that question; that is up to the officials to decide. I am talking about a person who has the eight-week qualification. If all things break in his favour, he can draw benefits for 44 weeks and he can do the same thing the following year. The minister and I have had good natured exchanges on this point in committee. He said that he assumes all Canadian people are honest and not lazy. I agree with the minister but I qualify the word "all"; I say some Canadian people would take advantage of the regulations. There is an old saw that anything you get from the government is not stolen. That is what will happen here. People will feel that if they have satisfied the minimum requirement and have worked the eight weeks, they can draw the benefits for 44 weeks and be within the law. It is the same thing as taking advantage of the loopholes in the Income Tax Act; that is not regarded as breaking the law.
I differ with the minister on this point. The hon.
member for Hamilton West made the point that if you dangle a carrot in front of a person's nose long enough he is going to snap it. I agree with him and that is what we are doing here. In most large cities, the department stores take on seasonal help. It is a common practice for
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
people to work several weeks around Christmas time, and then get laid off so that they can curl all winter. These people then go back to work for another seven or eight weeks in the spring, and get laid off again so they can golf all summer. While it is true there is an enforcement section in the act, I am using this illustration to point out what will happen if the rewards are made great enough that people do not mind cheating a little; it is not dishonest, it is cheating.
Another thing that bothers me about reducing the period to eight weeks is how it will affect students. I asked the officials whether a student who works eight weeks this summer, goes back to college in the fall and is ava lable for work again the following May probably for the balance of the year, could draw benefits as in the previous illustration. I was told that conceivably he could draw benefits up to 44 weeks. We all know the propensity of college students for travel and I can just see what will happen here. The student will say, "All right, I worked eight weeks last summer, I will take benefits for eight or twelve weeks and travel across the country". He can say that he will be available for work because he can get from Montreal to Toronto overnight if necessary. These are some of the abuses that can creep in when the plan is made so attractive. In committee one Liberal member said that we should be trying to help students. Of course we should, but this is not the way to do it. Let the government get the economy going to the point where we can give employment to students in summer and then they won't be tempted to take unemployment insurance benefits.
These are some of the reasons that I am in favour of this amendment to increase the qualifying period to 12 weeks, Mr. Speaker. I say again, it is only a judgment figure. I have not received any satisfactory explanation from the officials why eight weeks was chosen other than the fact that is the provision in the present act. I say it is not the same as the present act and, therefore, we could take any figure out of the hat. I feel that extending the period to 12 weeks, as my colleague has suggested in his amendment, would at least remove some of the dangers and ensure that those people who are applying for benefits are really in the labour force rather than just itinerant workers who work long enough to qualify and then draw benefits. By increasing the period to 12 weeks we would plug some of the loopholes that exist at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) because I believe it will help to restore to the proposed bill principles more in keeping with an insurance scheme than those measures now proposed by the government. In my opinion, the proposed act departs from the insurance principle by being universal and extending benefits to too many people who are basically not employed in the work force. If these people are to be assisted, and I think many of them should be, other vehicles are available and should be used to look after them.

June 10, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
Under the present Unemployment Insurance Act, and as stated on page 10 of the government's white paper on "Unemployment Insurance in the 70's", a claimant must have contributed to the unemployment insurance fund for at least 30 weeks over the preceding two 1-year period to qualify for benefits from it. The government now proposes to reduce this qualifying period or period of attachment to the labour force to eight weeks in any one year in order for a participant to receive benefits.
In its calculations of the cost of its new unemployment insurance plan, the government's financial assumptions were based on a national rate of unemployment of 4 per cent. Using this rate, it was estimated that the lowering of the eligibility period for the receipt of benefits would cost an extra 160 million dollars. Thus, even on a national basis of 4 per cent unemployment, a rate which we have not had for very nearly two years, by extending the proposed eligibility period from eight to 12 weeks, the government would be saving considerable money and could use it in other areas.
Even by increasing the eligibility period from eight to 12 weeks, Mr. Speaker, it will be entirely possible for someone to collect benefits from the unemployment insurance fund totally out of keeping with the government's publicly expressed desire to have an insurance scheme which will act as an incentive to work rather than the reverse. When one considers that most people in the country are engaged in tasks which are often unsatisfactory or unpleasant to them it seems to me that these people, with every good intention in the world, can use whatever means is available to make their lives happier.
As I recall, one of the reasons given during committee study of this bill for the government's removal of seasonal unemployment insurance benefits from the new act was that by lowering the eligibility period to eight weeks, a large measure of the need for seasonal unemployment insurance benefits would be eliminated. I would like to illustrate just how expensive an elimination this may well be by citing certain testimony which was brought out at the meeting of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration on May 5. The example which I shall cite concerns someone who works for as few as eight weeks a year, thus making him eligible for the receipt of benefits under the proposed new Unemployment Insurance Act. If he earns $150 during each of these eight weeks and pays into the fund a mere $1.19 weekly in premiums, which is the proposed new premium rate for the maximum weekly insurable earnings, or $9.52 for the eight weeks in which he works, he can draw a total of $4,000 in benefits from the fund.
The following exchange of remarks occurred at the committee meeting on May 5 between the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) and the general legal counsel to the unemployment insurance committee:
MR. Thomas (Moncton) : All right. I think Mr. Alexander will have an amendment. I will ask Mr. Steele or Mr. Douglas, one of the officials about a claimant who has the minor entitlement of eight weeks. If he has the entitlement, how many weeks benefits could he actually draw if he qualified for all phases of the situation, if at all?

speechtext: So if my arithmetic is correct, that gives a maximum of forty-four weeks, for eight weeks' work he could draw forty-four weeks benefits. He could work eight weeks this year, draw forty-four weeks benefits, conceivably he could work eight weeks next year and draw forty-four weeks benefits. Is that correct?

speechtext:
It would be possible if everything worked right for him.
Considering the application of this provision to my own area, I would like to point out that there are many farmers who must leave the land at the ages of 50, 55 or 60. They are still in good physical condition. They usually are not attached to the labour force. A farmer helping his neighbour with planting and harvesting would work slightly over eight weeks; that is the usual period in western Canada. This person could qualify for benefits. If the conditions were right, he could conceivably draw benefits for 44 weeks. Generally speaking, these people are not part of the work force. However, with this provision, it would be to their advantage to pay unemployment insurance in order to qualify for the extended benefits. With this in mind, I believe that the eligibility period of eight weeks is too short. It should be extended to at least 12 weeks. I do not disagree that there are some people who only work eight weeks who are in need of some help to sustain them through the year. However, for those people who consistently work only eight weeks a year, some other means must be found to assist them. In any event, the maximum benefit of 44 weeks is not enough to see them through the year. Therefore, I hope the House will see its way clear to support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on the amendment.
I will say right away that I am not quite in agreement with the sponsor. One could ask: why not two, three, four, twelve or fifteen weeks?
To my mind, the bill in its present form really fits into the context. After listening to comments of some hon. members I am under the impression that there has not been sufficient recognition of the present context. The department is now making a commendable effort, in keeping with the unemployment problem we now face.
I also recognize that some individuals would be tempted to work only eight weeks to obtain benefits during 44

June 10, 1971

weeks. If I was assured that the bill would be in effect during 10, 15 or 20 years, I would probably object to such a clause. However, I think that the present situation was taken into account and considering the difficulties which we are experiencing-I imagine that it is always possible to annul the bill with the approval of the House-it is quite acceptable under the cirmum-stances.
I wonder if it would not be advisable to ask the minister to consider seriously the situation, in order not to tempt workers to work eight weeks to be entitled to 44 weeks of benefits.
It would be to the advantage of the minister and the government to consider, in the future, requiring a given type of work for a given benefit. I believe that is where the problem lies. If we continue to increase unemployment insurance benefits, we are tempting the people and we are inviting them to take the line of least resistance. And that is dangerous.
Always within the present context, I believe that this clause is acceptable, but I must take advantage of this opportunity to tell the minister that any work that is of benefit to society should be considered. Municipalities and provinces would find it useful, I think, to enter into agreements with the federal government for certain projects that are urgently needed and that they cannot afford to carry out alone.
If we keep on constantly increasing unemployment insurance benefits and relaxing the requirements, we shall be responsible, for instance, for spoiling a generation because we are inviting them to abuse their rights. We must be careful not to allow the people to get the benefits too easily.
Considering the present context and the difficulties we know, this clause of the bill is acceptable in 1971 and I hope we shall be able through the co-operation of hon. members to set up some programs and projects in consultation with provinces and municipalities so that benefits will always be available.
We shall better serve the interests of the nation by ensuring a fair distribution of benefits, but it is still alarming and annoying for the people who work all their lives to see others collect benefits so easily.
Indeed, some workers wonder why they spend their lives working, year after year, while others manage to survive without doing so.
To my mind, even though they will be increased, unemployment benefits will still not be high for many people. I think most Canadian workers have more ambition than that and always try to work.
Still, the limit of eight weeks is logical. Surely, with a much lower rate of unemployment, we could perhaps increase these requirements to 12 or 15 weeks. But I believe that for the moment, these eight weeks are welcome and we will try and demand a minimum of work for the good of society rather than give more in return for lesser requirements.
In closing my remarks, I would say that I am in favour of the clause dealing with the qualifying period.

That Bill S-12, an act respecting Central-Del Rio Oils Limited, be amended by adding the following to clause 1 at line 27 on page 1:
"on the condition that sections 52 to 56 of the Bank Act apply to the company mutatls mutandis notwithstanding the provisions of part I of the Canada Corporations Act."
He said: Mr. Speaker-
Same old speech.

-those who believe in Canadian ownership and want to ensure that this country has Canadian ownership, particularly to preserve as such companies that are now Canadian, make the same old speech from time to time and those who are opposed, like some of my Liberal friends, either make a speech in favour of the sort of speech you would expect from those interested in selling. Then it all depends how much they can get for it; it is a tradeable commodity. I am happy to have my speech bear the stamp of "Same old speech" because we in this party have always been in favour of Canadian ownership and thus it is a pleasure to come before the House today to ask for certain considerations in this regard.
My colleague the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) would want to indicate that we apply to this company the provisions of Sections 52 to 56 of the Bank Act that are laid out in the Canadian statutes. Because of expediency, as well as necessity, the Bank Act provided that foreign-owned banking institutions in this country would be permitted, but foreign-owned banks-and there was a small one in Canada at that time-were to be given a number of alternatives. The Bank Act also provided that a particular bank or company could decide whether it would remain a small investment organization in this country or, alternatively, take a ten-year period to expand very rapidly with the intention of disposing of their operation at the end of that time.
The Bank Act was worded in that way to permit an honest transfer of stock to Canadian shareholders. It allowed the company to make a reasonable profit on their banking ventures in Canada because for a ten-year period they were able to take advantage of expansions of the market and of the provisions of the act. Then they were given the opportunity to sell the operation at a reasonable profit. Those involved in passing the amendments to the Bank Act were of the opinion that the banking institutions of Canada were so important to our development and to the operation of this country as a nation that they wrote into the act these concessions in response to the decision that we had made that the banking institutions of Canada must at all times be under the control of the Parliament of Canada and must react in a predictable way to the policies of the Bank of Canada.
This has been an acceptable position. It is not the kind of position that would be taken in countries which nationalize industries for the sake of nationalization. It did allow for the orderly expansion of the operation concerned. If companies decided to remain in this coun-

June 10, 1971

try with modest growth so they would retain a very small portion of the financial market, then they would be able to do so. However, if they wanted to get the benefit of the normal financial expansion that they could expect if they were allowed to use their banking skills to increase their operations in Canada, then they could do so provided they sold the operation after ten years.
I agree with those who may speak on this subject later and say that the application of the Bank Act to this particular company does make for a ponderous type of legislation in that it takes into consideration some of the difficulties that develop in financial institutions, the fact that financial institutions often have lending problems that may extend over a period of years, and the difficulty of orderly liquidation in the market. This may not apply to this particular company, but we have had companies come before us which on a voluntary basis, with the prodding of the sponsor, the prodding of Members of Parliament and the knowledge of several other companies that they were operating in Canada in a field that was of importance to the development of the economy and resources of our nation, made the concession to members of this party, who for a long time have been interested in Canadian control of our development and of our institutions, that they would remain Canadian and would make this a condition of their incorporation.
There have been other companies-not numerous, unfortunately-which have voluntarily made the concession that if granted the incorporation they were asking for they would make a commitment to Parliament and to the corporate affairs department responsible for our corporate structure that if they did not become 50 per cent Canadian-owned, at the end of the ten-year period they would relinquish their charter and cease to exist as a corporate entity under federal law.
I admit that I do not know whether the corporate structure that we have established in Canada, particularly the provisions of the Corporations Act, has the machinery to ascertain in a meaningful way whether or not companies are Canadian. I am not sure whether companies are in a position to know whether 50 per cent of the stock is in the hands of Canadians normally resident in Canada or whether in their shareholdings there are holding companies which meet the criterion of Canadian-resident ownership yet are in fact controlled from outside the country. In my opinion we have not given consideration to devising a method of ascertaining the nominal control of a company through the stock procedures we allow in Canada. We do not have the machinery necessary to make this assessment and do something about it.
Representatives of this company appeared before the committee and made several commitments. I am not aware whether those commitments have been carried out. If you lcok at the Financial Post survey on oils for 1971 you find that this company has a number of wholly-owned subsidiaries, an interest in more than 705 million net acres of oil rights and 20 million net acres in oil and gas rights, chiefly in western and northern Canada. As of
Central-Del Rio Oils Limited
October, 1969, these companies had issued 20 million shares through Canadian Pacific Investments Limited for all the issued and outstanding shares of Canadian Pacific Oil and Gas Limited.
The purpose of this bill is to amalgamate Central-Del Rio Oils Limited and Canadian Pacific Oil and Gas Limited. They would be amalgamated under the Canada Corporations Act, with the shareholders' approval to be sought at a subsequent annual meeting. The shareholders of this company are at this stage, from my reading of-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Why don't you say it from memory?

I have not been closely connected with the oil industry long enough to name the board of directors without at least looking them up. I suppose the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) could do this. He would say that former Premier Manning is probably a director of every oil company in western Canada. He has been well rewarded. I suppose he would say that Duff Roblin could reasonably be expected to be on the board of directors of this and every other oil company in western Canada.
Then it would become a little more difficult because you run out of premiers. In reading the list of the executive of various oil companies I cannot find the name of a former premier of Saskatchewan. This may be an oversight or it may reflect to some extent the policy of the Saskatchewan government and its interest in having Canadian ownership and Canadian rights in the hands of Canadians. This is particularly so in respect of oil companies on a provincial basis. I suppose the other provinces were not so fussy. In reading this list of directors I find the names of both gentleman whom I mentioned. It is interesting to note that the address of Hon. Duff Roblin is listed as Montreal, rather than Manitoba, but I presume it is the same person. It is also interesting to note that Mr. Taylor is president of this company and several subsidiaries.
It is surprising that a few years ago this company was almost entirely owned or controlled by Canadian Pacific Investments Limited, which was operating almost entirely on pension moneys of the workers of Canadian Pacific Railway. This very large sum of money represented Canadian investment of a very basic kind.
This bill was considered by the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and by the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. It is to be noted that the Canadian Pacific Railway pension funds constituted, I suppose, a controlling interest in this company. Suddenly the fund did not appear to represent a major investment in this company. This fact gives rise to the problem referred to by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. He noticed that there was a change almost overnight. The fund did not represent a major investment in a Canadian-owned operation, but an operation held or controlled by another company.
We believe, as I hope some Liberals-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Don't count on it.

-and some Conservatives do, that a company which is involved in a resource-based industry in

June 10, 1971
Central-Del Rio Oils Limited this nation should play a very important role in the development of our natural resources. We also believe, as I am sure most members do, that if a company is Canadian-owned it will play a role consistent with the wishes and aspirations of the Canadian public at large.
I am well aware that we are asking a great deal of the people who control Canadian corporations operating our development industries, in that they operate side by side with United States corporations involved in industries of which they have no particular knowledge or interest except profit making. I am sure most members agree that a Canadian appointed as president, as we have in the case of Central-Del Rio Oils Limited, will be interested in ecology, conservation and the orderly development of a corporate structure operating in the resource fields and will represent to a greater extent the aspirations of the Canadian nation in this regard than will the president of a United States or a foreign-owned corporation.
There have been changes in the shareholders and in the operations of this company. Mr. Taylor, as president of Central-Del Rio, could not give the assurance that the shareholders would remain Canadian. He could not give a commitment that the board of directors would remain Canadian. I suggest that the decision to have this company under the control and direction of Canadian nationalists can only be made by Parliament. If we include in this bill those sections of the Bank Act which apply to control and ownership by foreign corporations we will have decided that as long as this corporation is under the Canada Corporations Act it will reflect the aspirations of Canadian nationals and will be controlled by Canadians.
I suggest that many members of this House would agree that Canadian ownership is an important factor in the development of a resource-based area. I refer particularly to hon. members who have been connected with the mining industry and the oil industry. They know that many companies which are buying up Canadian resources do not have any interest in the development of our natural resources. These companies have no interest in or knowledge of the development role they should play in terms of the relationship of the commodity they are producing to the needs of the nation.
When a United States company buys up or obtains control of such a corporation its only motive, and rightly so, is to derive a profit from the resource. Why should a large United States corporation not buy an oil company which will produce a return of 7 per cent, 8 per cent, 10 per cent or 12 per cent on its investment? Why should it be concerned about whether or not it is exploiting the country in which it operates? I do not blame these people a bit. But representing a portion of the Canadian people, I believe I have a responsibility to take every opportunity-and such opportunity arises when company incorporations come up for consideration-to ensure the retention of ownership of industry in the hands of the Canadian public.
There are those who have said, and correctly so, that many entrepreneurs in Canada are engaged in buying up
lucrative portfolios. They are not all foreigners. I have seen it in my own area, where Little Longlac gold mine-a little, two-bit company-moved into Kirkland Lake and bought the Lakeshore mine. This company drew out all the Lakeshore profits and closed the mine. I am not familiar with the company or its board of directors, but I can say they are as much scavengers as any foreign-owned company could be. I want to curtail that kind of operation in respect of any company which comes before us, particularly in the area of our resources. For this reason 1 commend and support the amendment of the hon. member for Moose Jaw.

Mr. Speaker, it could be said that we are pouring oil on troubled waters, but you know from past experience that when my colleagues in the New Democratic Party speak on this subject, they speak with persuasiveness and strength. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) is very important, not only to the members of the New Democratic Party but to Canadians at large. I am delighted to see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) in the House, because he comes from Calgary, Alberta. I am also delighted to see our football star, who is also a member from Calgary. I am sure they wish to participate in this debate.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I am not from Calgary but, rather, from Edmonton.

I apologize to the hon. member. I am sure these gentlemen will listen very attentively to the comments of my colleagues and will probably participate in the debate.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to present an historical and constructive point of view on this matter. I recall in the early 1960s a voice from the wilderness. I refer to Walter Gordon who sensed the problem of Canadian ownership. He wrote a book. He attempted to take some action because he appreciated the problem of foreign ownership. Unfortunately, his voice was not heard. He left the Liberal cabinet. The result is that we have seen an increasing trend toward foreign ownership. I shall not repeat in detail the tremendous United States and foreign penetration that has taken place in the Canadian economy, particularly in oil fields and natural resources. Surely the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance could do it far more ably than I and I am sure he will be glad to do it.
On its face this bill would appear to be innocent. According to the explanatory notes the purpose is simply to permit the company to be continued as a company incorporated under the Canada Corporations Act. Then the explanatory notes read.
The company will be permitted to carry out in Canada its existing objects. If the shareholders approve of an application to continue the company as a company incorporated under the Canada Corporations Act, any amalgamation agreement thereafter adopted by the shareholders shall be deemed to be an amalgamation agreement for the purposes of such act, provided that the agreement complies with certain requirements of section 128A of such act.

June 10, 1971

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) pointed out the valiant attempts this party has made to retain Canadian content in companies and more especially companies which may be subject to foreign control. The easy approach to this question would be for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) to bring forward an amendment to the Canada Corporations Act which would include what is set forth in the Bank Act, which is the substance of the amendment of the hon. member for Moose Jaw.
When I came here in 1965 I was made a member of the finance committee when it was studying the Bank Act. The question of foreign ownership came up because of the operations of the Mercantile Bank in Canada. I recall the Minister of Labour playing his usual important part in going down to New York and speaking to Mr. Rockefeller. He pointed out to him how necessary it was to retain Canadian ownership of our banks. The result was that Mr. Rockefeller appeared before the committee and gave evidence.
Then amendments were made to sections 52 to 57 of the Bank Act to the effect that any non-resident may hold up to 10 per cent of the shares in a Canadian bank, but that the total number of shares of a non-resident may not exceed 25 per cent. We in the New Democratic Party feel that although other measures should be taken to regain control of our economy, the measure set forth by the hon. member for Moose Jaw is a step in the right direction. In other words, if it is good enough for the banks it should be good enough for other Canadian companies. This is why the amendment has been brought forward. When the hon. member attempted to bring it forward in the committee he was met with strong objection from some members and did not have the opportunity to present it. The reason he is bringing it forth is to persuade hon. members that it is a vital amendment which should receive the acceptance of all members of the House.
On various occasions I have asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) when he will bring forth his report concerning foreign ownership. He has, to put it midly, delayed making a definite commitment on when this legislation will be brought forth. I, like many Canadians, feel that by the time it is brought forth we will be in a far worse position regarding foreign ownership in Canada than we are today, because foreign penetration is increasing rapidly.
As the former leader of my party puts it, we do not mind our U.S. cousins coming to Canada to visit us, but we would like to stay in the house rather than move to the garage. It appears that Canadians are being moved to the garage while our guests are taking over control of the house. That trend should be stopped. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) brings forth his budget on Friday, June 18, I am sure he will have in mind the tax impact that oil companies have on the Canadian economy. When you study the effects that our tax laws have on oil companies, with their tax holidays, depletion allowances and all the advantages that accrue to them,
Central-Del Rio Oils Limited
you realize how important it is not only to change the tax laws but to change the corporate laws of our country to protect Canadian ownership.
I notice that the parliamentary secretary is listening attentively. He has a wealth of information and experience and I am sure he looks forward to the budget and to what may happen with regard to oil companies and the tax policy. But more important than that is the key question of ownership. I have yet to discover any country that has laws which permit the penetration into their economy that prevails in Canada. When you look at Sweden and Japan you see that when they borrow money for purposes of developing their economy they do it on a loan capital basis rather than on an equity basis. It is high time that we in Canada took the same approach.
If a commentary were written about the former Premier of Alberta, it would be much like that written of Esau-that he sold the natural resources of Canada for a mess of pottage. As Canadians we should see that Esau's conduct is not repeated in Canada; and the former Premier of Alberta being rewarded with a seat in the Senate is not what Canadians want. That is why the hon. member for Moose Jaw is to be commended for his approach to this problem.
I note that the former Solicitor General is present. He has been in the House for more than 30 years and has greatly contributed to the well-being of Canadians. He has been in the forefront of many social measures and I am sure that if he were given the opportunity to become Minister of Finance one of the first steps he would take would be to impose tax laws which would protect Canadian ownership. If he were Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs I am sure the first step he would take would be to adopt the same approach that we took under the Bank Act and have it applied mutatis mutandis. The hon. member knows the real meaning of that phrase; it means "to the same effect".

not only to the Bank Act but to the Corporations Act.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: It means tit for tat.

I believe the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) is asking what I mean by mutatis mutandis. It is a legal, Latin phrase which has an important meaning. The meaning that we want to apply here is the one included in the Bank Act, that a non-resident of Canada should be confined to 10 per cent of the ownership of a Canadian company and ownership by a group of non-residents should not exceed 25 per cent.
I am sure it is not necessary for me to continue. The hon. member for Timiskaming has been so persuasive that I feel I am being repetitive. I am sure that other hon. members will support us.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on Bill S-12, an act respecting Central-Del Rio Oils Limited. In reading the legislation I believe there are several points which should be put on record. Anyone checking the record of the committee proceedings which

June 10, 1971
Central-Del Rio Oils Limited
took place on May 20, 1971-the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications-will understand why members of my party are apprehensive about the way in which the bill is presently drafted.
We are seeking an amendment to the legislation which will guarantee that this corporation will remain under Canadian control. We do not have to apologize to anyone for the fight we are putting up for Canadian control of our economy. We have been talking about it ever since our party was formed. We will continue to preach this philosophy until Canadians wake up to the fact that we are rapidly losing control of our economy and that once you lose control of your economy, you also lose political control.
I would like to tell members of the House what Central-Del Rio Oils Limited really is and the extent of its holdings in Canada. Questions were asked in the committee of those who were presenting the bill and I should like to read into the record part of the proceedings of the committee. Mr. Beaven was speaking. He spoke about Central-Del Rio Oils Limited and said:
Mr. Chairman, I have some figures here. Central-Del Rio Oils Limited is controlled to the extent of 89.27 per cent by Canadian Pacific Investments Limited, which in turn is a subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Our shareholdings are divided as follows. This was at December 11, 1970, and there has been no significant change. We had a total of 8,374 shareholders, of which approximately 7,200 were corporations and individuals resident in Canada holding in the aggregate just about 30 million shares out of an issue of about 30.5 million. We had 999 shareholders who were individuals and corporations resident in the United States holding in the aggregate 390,000 shares. This is out of 30 million shares. The remaining 128 shareholders were individuals and corporations residing outside of Canada and the United States and holding in the aggregate 319,000 shares. So, of the just over 30 million shares which are issued and outstanding, 29,800,000 are held by residents of Canada.
That is a very satisfying statement and no one would object to it. It is an excellent record and we want to see it maintained. The following question was asked by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg):
What assurance is there in the bill before us that this company, your Central-Del Rio, would not become predominantly owned by U.S. shareholders or outside shareholders-I will not say U.S.; I will say shareholders outside of Canada? Is there anything in the bill right now before us that would spell out in clarity that this company will remain predominantly owned by Canadian investors?
The answer by Mr. Taylor was:
No. there is nothing in the bill which spells out that. We cannot give our firm assurance that we will not have foreign shareholders so long as we are listed on the Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver stock exchanges. But we can give you the assurance that the ownership in the company by Canadian Pacific Investments will never be less than an appreciable percentage above 50 per cent.
This is the very point that our members are trying to make. While the company is predominantly owned by shareholders in Canada, there is absolutely no guarantee that this situation will remain unchanged. That is the crux of the debate and gave rise to the amendment we
have placed before the House. In the context of that answer I should like to read the amendment:
That Bill S-12, an act respecting Central-Del Rio Oils Limited, be amended by adding the following to clause 1 at line 27 on page 1:
"on the condition that sections 52 to 56 of the Bank Act apply to the company mutatis mutandis notwithstanding the provisions of part I of the Canada Corporations Act."
What does this mean? It means that if the amendment is accepted we will never lose Canadian control of this company. This is something in which all members of the House should be interested. We should be taking steps to make certain that Canadian control is retained over a corporation such as this. We have had debates in this House about Canadian ownership. Those debates will continue. They will spill over into the next election campaign. The Canadian people are beginning to realize that this is one of the major issues facing our nation.
As has already been pointed out, much of the resource development that should be taking place in Canada is not taking place, principally because we have lost control of the resource-based industries. Canada is used as a supply house for industries which are located elsewhere. When bills such as this come before the House of Commons we will seek amendment of them to assure retention of Canadian control of our natural resources.
Anyone who notes the tremendous acreage controlled by this company must be alarmed. We must take the necessary precautions to ensure that it remains under Canadian control. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) told us about some of the holdings which the company has in northern Canada. I understand it is one of the group participating with Panarctic Oils in the exploration of the Arctic Islands, and just the other day we learned that one of the biggest gas finds in history was made in the north. Foreign corporations must be interested when they see that a company like this has an interest in that kind of discovery. It is up to us as Canadians to protect the company.
There are one or two other points that I would like to make with respect to this company's holdings in the various provinces. Again I shall quote from the committee proceedings. Those who appeared on behalf of the company were asked what holdings they had in the province of Saskatchewan, for example. This passage is recorded in the minutes of May 20:
-I see that under the affiliated company, Minerals Limited, Saskatchewan Incorporated owns 20 per cent of the minerals underlying approximately 750,000 acres

These amendments were introduced by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander).

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I am always at a tremendous disadvantage in debating with charming people. I have been sitting here quietly admiring his technique most of the afternoon. He is one of the few members who can, with
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
some confidence in success, play both sides of the street when it comes to moving amendments. Both he and the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) are very knowledgeable persons by reason of their active participation in the committee.
The hon. member for Moncton has suggested that this bill is not consistent. Although I think that is a matter of opinion, I would suggest that any amendments that have been brought in today have done nothing to remove the inconsistency if there is one. A good example of this is when on one hand we suggest a reduction of the two-week waiting period to one week, at a cost of $160 million or more, and then two minutes later introduce another amendment which would in effect negate what the original amendment was supposed to be doing, namely, help the workers, by increasing the qualifying period from eight weeks to 12 weeks. This would mean that several hundred thousand workers every year who had eight weeks qualifying attachment to the work force but less than 12 weeks-be it 9, 10 or 11 weeks- would not qualify for benefits. We have estimated that this would affect a quarter of a million people who through no fault of their own find themselves temporarily without earnings and who would be ineligible for unemployment insurance.
We talked today about a question of judgment. Before we get into that question I think the whole of this proposed program, as opposed to the basic philosophy of the present program, was to insure members of the work force against the probability of financial loss on those occasions when they are temporarily without work. This is fundamentally different from the old plan where, in effect, your number of weeks benefit was geared or related to your work attachment. In other words, more often than not under the existing plan the people best able to survive or to exist without any income usually find that unemployment insurance benefits come more easily to them and for longer periods than those who need them more by reason of their underemployment or the fact that they are in and out of the work force fairly frequently.
What has pleased me in all of the contributions made in respect of this amendment is that all hon. members have said, I am sure sincerely, that the average Canadian is not lazy. Certainly I have never heard the hon. member for Hamilton West make such a statement and I am sure it would be a distortion of his words if it appeared in print that way. Nevertheless, I wholeheartedly agree with the hon. member for Moncton that human nature being what it is, some people will try to abuse unemployment insurance no matter what the qualifying period is.
To say, for example, that a person who has eight weeks attachment to the work force and then stops work and draws benefit for 44 weeks is to oversimplify the plan. It is true that some people with eight weeks attachment to the work force could draw 44 weeks under certain conditions. The same is true of a man with 9, 10, 11 or 12 weeks attachment. But if you had eight weeks attachment you could easily plan your work pattern to stop at, say, 12 weeks and then draw 44 weeks benefit.

June 10, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) got a little excited about that proposition.
However, I do not think that life insurance, for example, is any less consistent in its approach. After all, a man could be unfortunate enough to drop dead after paying the first premium. What we are saying in this bill, in effect, is that there will be some members of the work force who after 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12 weeks in the work force may be unfortunate enough to find themselves out of work and will draw benefits. However, since the plan is actuarially sound, the probability of this happening is such that, in general, due to the universal coverage of the fund we will be able to absorb the payment of benefits to the number of people who could theoretically draw from the fund for 44 weeks following an initial eight weeks attachment.
I am sure that no one wants to leave the wrong impression on the record. I must underline that you do not automatically draw 44 weeks' benefits after an attachment to the work force of eight weeks. You are entitled to eight weeks' benefits, but from there on it all depends on the economic conditions in the particular region of the country concerned. Since we are trying to help a person financially during the period in which he is out of work, it is only logical that we should extend the period of benefit in relationship to the probability of that person being reabsorbed into the work force. The probability of his being absorbed into the work force is directly related to the rate of unemployment in the country and in his particular community.
All other things being equal, people are better working than not working. I have met very few people who would rather draw unemployment insurance than work. Perhaps I am naive or idealistic, but I am of the view-and most hon. members have said the same thing-that the overwhelming majority of Canadians are honest. We must not lose sight of the fact that a man who quits work at the end of the eighth week has a waiting period, one some hon. members think is too long, before he can draw benefits. He must be interviewed and be ready, willing and able to work. He will be subject to the discipline of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and to the spot checks that they make and to visits to the home.
Neither can we lose sight of the fact that 86,000 people last year were disqualified because they were not ready, willing and able to work. Indeed, the Unemployment Insurance Commission are doing their job zealously, to the point that at times we are asked whether they are not being overzealous in making sure that only people eligible for unemployment insurance draw from the fund.
Then the question came up as to why we had chosen eight weeks and not 12. When we put together our model on the computers when this plan was first visualized, we took a sampling of some 250,000 people in the work force. The economists, both internal economists and those hired to work with the group, worked on this model of 250,000 as representative of the five million people in the work force, which is a larger than average sampling for this type of study. As a result of this sampling we found that with eight weeks we were able to do all the things we
wanted to do in the act with regard to the relationship between benefits and salaries, periodical extensions of the benefit structure in relation to the unemployment pattern in the country, sickness and maternity benefits, and so on. All these proposals are feasible with an eight weeks attachment period to the work force.
Let me come back to make the point that if the period were set at 12 weeks it would not in any way reduce the number of people who are dishonest enough intentionally to try to defraud the fund. We have other ways of preventing this. Neither would such a period in any way change the system of interviews or the necessity for people to be ready, willing and able to work. No one knows when spot checks will be made or when telephone calls will be put through to find out whether a man is in or out of the city, or is ready, willing and able to do a job that Manpower may have available for him.
e (8:20 p.m.)
It is not just a matter of being attached to the work force for eight weeks and deciding to draw benefits for 44 weeks. It means attached to the work force for at least eight weeks and then being legitimately unemployed. That means waiting two weeks and drawing benefits for eight weeks. It means that at the end of eight weeks the situation is assessed and evaluated in light of unemployment figures in the region and in the nation, then assessing the probabilities of the man finding work with that rate of unemployment. If, according to the formula, it is highly probable that work is not easy to find because of the burden of unemployment, this is taken into1 consideration and the period is extended. It is not fair on the part of hon. members to leave on the record the presumption that one can automatically draw 44 weeks' benefits.
We then get into the question of students. This is a problem in our country and it is hard to rationalize the arguments I sometimes hear against students drawing unemployment insurance, as though they were second-class citizens. They are not. If a student leaves university in May and goes to work in a legitimate business the same as his father, brother or people in the normal work force, pays unemployment insurance, goes back to university in the fall and comes back to the work force the following May and cannot find work, provided he has the specified attachment-which is eight weeks or more- there is no reason why he should not draw unemployment insurance just because he happens to be a student eight months of the year. If we find work for him, he must work. If he is not ready, willing and able to work, then he does not draw unemployment insurance.
If students want to travel across Canada, take advantage of other forms of summer activities, go to Europe or do one of the many things students want to do today, they are not eligible for unemployment insurance. On the other hand, if they want to stay and are eligible for work, ready, willing and able, and society cannot provide them with jobs, it is not the fault of the students. If they have paid their stamps and are eligible in every other way. shape and form, there is no reason why they should not be allowed to draw unemployment insurance like every other citizen in this country.
[Mr. Mackasey.l

speechtext: I find nothing wrong or ridiculous about this. I think it will go a long way to help provide some form of income for students who are not as affluent as others and who do not have wealthy fathers to provide pin money.
