speechtext: Don't look at me.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I am disqualifying myself by saying "wealthy fathers." I think we all know that some people are more affluent than others. This will, incidentally, answer the question about students graduating or coming out of teachers college after two years, who work for the summer months and go back to university. If they are unable to again join the work force the following summer, they should draw unemployment insurance in relation, of course, to the number of weeks to which they are entitled.
I do not want to become too political about this, but I should point out to the hon. member for Hamilton West that you cannot have it all ways. You cannot in one amendment reflect the thinking of the CMA, in the next amendment reflect the thinking of the CLC and in the next amendment reflect the thinking of the Chamber of Commerce. If you have a philosophy it should be consistent all through your amendments. Let me say this to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). His philosophy or ideology may not be the same as ours, but at least he is consistent. I think consistency is a virtue in this day and age.
Let me say in conclusion that I think there is nothing wrong with the eight-week waiting period. I listened objectively today for one good reason why the amendment should be accepted, making the eligibility period 12 weeks instead of eight weeks. There is nothing in this to offset many of the possible abuses mentioned during the debate. The amendment does nothing to prevent a dishonest person attempting to defraud the fund. At the end of eight weeks he would be as dishonest as he would be at the end of 12. He may just have to wait longer to try his luck.
I think the eight weeks period makes sense, particularly in light of the large work force in Canada and the fact that so many young people are coming into the work force for the first time. Our experience over the last five years indicates that several hundred thousand workers each year are ineligible for unemployment insurance because they have not accumulated a sufficiently long attachment to the work force to be eligible.
We have a tendency to criticize our welfare agencies. We should be honest about the alternative to unemployment insurance. If you are not eligible and have no other income, there is the Canada Assistance Plan. If you draw money from the Canada Assistance Plan you become a financial burden upon your community, the towns and cities, and you become a financial burden on the province which pays half the cost of the Canada Assistance Plan. It is very difficult for young men to find work even under the best of circumstances. It is twice as hard if at the
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 same time they are living on welfare. I think we all know and agree with that.
One of the legitimate features of this plan is that it at least postpones the day when you have to turn to the Canada Assistance Plan for financial assistance. It postpones the day by providing higher benefits with easier eligibility. In this way we give a man an opportunity to seek work while he still has the dignity of an income. Welfare should not be looked down upon by society, but unfortunately it is.
I would ask the House to reject the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton West.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always like to hear my good friend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) take part in a debate because he has the ability of being very personable and being loved by all sides. He is one of those fellows who, when he sees the debate going one way and needs a little support, analyses the philosophy of an hon. member or a party and then makes a great appeal and is very complimentary, as he was with one member, although he was somewhat critical of another.
I am not worried about being personable in my feeling about the question of eight weeks or 12 weeks as the attachment period. What I am concerned about is the hypocrisy in calling this act an Unemployment Insurance Act. I listened this afternoon to the Minister of Labour and other hon. members speaking about insurance. As I understand insurance, when you pay the premium you are insured. After you have paid a few premiums and the commission to the agent-and I never overlook that-you are insured and your policy will build up a cash value.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: That is private insurance.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I am talking about private insurance. That is what the Minister of Labour was talking about. What the Minister has done under this act is include a lot of people to pay for the plan. That is why there should be a 12-week period rather than an eight-week period. He is bringing in a lot of people who will never benefit. When one takes out life insurance-there are various types of plans, which I am not here to discuss-you are gambling with the company as to whether you are going to live. You build up a cash value and dividends, unless it is short-term and that is very cheap insurance. Right from the beginning of the old plan, thousands of Canadians who have contributed have never drawn a dollar.

will appreciate what we are talking about. Clause 17 provides, and this is what we are talking about:
An insured person qualifies to receive benefits under this act if he (a) has had eight or more weeks of insurable employment in his qualifying period-
When you shorten the time, the plan will cost more because you are bringing more people under it. That is the point I am making and that is the argument I am answering so far as the Minister of Labour is concerned. I am sorry if the Chair thought my remarks were not relevant. I am saying that by extending this plan you are bringing in school teachers and other people who have never been under it before, including thousands and thousands of Canadians who will never draw a dollar out of the fund.
The hon. member for Hamilton West is attempting to ease the problem by changing the period from 8 weeks to 12 weeks. It will cost the country less money, because under the policies of this government-I hope you think this is relevant, Mr. Speaker-if people are unemployed, whether they have 8 weeks or 12 weeks they will be on unemployment insurance for some time. The percentage of unemployment is so high at this time that a large number of people will need help under this act, and when they run out of benefits they will require social assistance. As I see it, the reason for the amendment is to make the act as reasonable as possible. The Minister of Labour is bringing in thousands and thousands of Canadians who will never benefit. Do you think the teachers of the country want this legislation, or the nurses-

speechtext: Yes.

The minister says yes. His mail is different from mine. I am prepared to send him 3,000 or
4,000	answers to questions I asked of school teachers and others. These people have not been covered and do not want coverage. This amendment is really an attempt to relieve the situation; that is the purpose behind it. The Minister of Labour talks about an insurance plan, when it would seem to me that he is bringing in a new tax. I say to the members of the NDP that there will be less take-home pay for many of the people they represent. There will also be less profit to people who hire workers, and there will be a higher cost to the consumer. If the NDP wants to go for a higher cost to the consumer, then I agree with what one minister said the other day, namely, that you cannot have it both ways. If you increase the cost of production, you have to increase the cost to the producer.

speechtext: The hon. member says, "Very little". Let us get down to sound economics. We change the Canada Pension Plan, we increase the surtax and income tax, we increase unemployment insurance deductions from industrial concerns and management, and then we increase the cost of labour, widen the scope and increase taxes.

speechtext: Would the hon. member explain, for my benefit, how there is a difference in the cost to the consumer between paying under an insurance plan and paying taxes levied under a welfare plan, if he is talking about the total cost to our society?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
That is one of the most intelligent questions that has been asked. So long as this government is creating unemployment, I agree that there is not much difference. But let us not play games. This is not an insurance plan at all; it is really a new system of taxing the Canadian people. This is the point I am making. I see an hon. member opposite shake his head. He shakes his head whenever anyone on this side speaks. If the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) told him at supper time to go for a swim, he would go for a swim. I am glad the big fellow, the acting House leader, has left because he can never understand logic.
With reference to the amendment, when you increase the period from 8 weeks to 12 weeks at least you are cutting down the cost of this kind of insurance, if you can call it insurance at all. So it is basically a compromise between the position of the minister and the position of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). Let us make no mistake about it: this is a brand new tax against Canadians-not only against the workers but against the employers. That is what it is all about. This legislation is dragged in to cover up unemployment caused deliberately by the nineteenth century economic policies of the government.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak very briefly on this amendment. At the outset may I say that I intend to oppose the amendment brought in by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). It does not make any sense to tell the unemployed of Canada that we are bringing in a new act in which the limit is set at eight weeks after which they can draw benefits, and then have someone tell us it should be increased to 12 weeks. I bebeve the question asked was very much to the point. If people who are unemployed do not receive money from unemployment insurance, they will obtain it from welfare. Don't try to kid yourselves that this money will not come out of the pockets of the taxpayers.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.

We believe that if a worker can receive some income from the unemployment insurance fund or pension scheme it is much better for him to have this money as of right than to get it from welfare. This is something the workers understand. They at least have tried to work and have made their contribution to the fund, and this money should come to them as of right. Whether or not the members of the Conservative party understand it, there is a big difference between welfare and unemployment insurance.

There are only a few comments I wish to make. The impression was left earlier that all some workers had to do was work for eight weeks and somehow or other they would be laid off, following which they would be able to draw benefits for the balance of the year. The minister has very ably explained the situation in which unemployed workers will receive benefits. I will not repeat it, but I want to make my position crystal clear. The impression has been left that the maximum amount is $100 a week under this legislation, but the number of unemployed workers receiving $100 a week will be very limited. A vast number of unemployed people will be much below the $7,800 a year income bracket which would give them the $100 a week benefit.
There is another point which I do not think has been made by anyone else in this debate. For the first time, unemployed workers have to pay income tax on their
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 benefits. This takes another big chunk out of the increased benefits which they will receive under the legislation. The point I am making is that the benefits which people will receive after eight weeks or more will certainly not be all gravy because there are taxes and charges against them. They have to pay the unemployment insurance contribution.
To leave the impression that workers will deliberately leave a job to draw unemployment insurance is wrong: I think it is an unfair statement to make about the Canadian work force. It does not matter where you go, whether it is in business or any other industrial activity there is always someone who will swing the lead, but generally the vast majority of our people want jobs; they will work if they can get jobs. This is the kind of protection that we should give to the working people of Canada. I am surprised that the Tory party would bring in such an amendment at this time when there are vast numbers of unemployed in our nation. I have no hesitation in saying that I intend to vote against the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the persuasive arguments of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) and of the last speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), I shall take only a few minutes to speak against the amendment.
I have heard the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) try to compare private insurance with unemployment insurance. In trying to draw an analogy he pointed out that private life insurance includes protection and savings. The immediate question that arose in my mind was, what happens to the savings when a person dies? He never collects them. The only time he collects his savings under a life insurance plan is when he surrenders the policy during his lifetime. This is one of the harsh criticisms which should be made against life insurance companies. It is term insurance, it is protection; and this act provides protection.
May I give my wonderful friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), a little bit of political advice and remind him that back in 1948 when we attempted to pass one of the main social measures in Canada, namely the family allowance legislation, the leader of his party called it iniquitous.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of my involvement in this debate I think I have made my mark because not only the minister, on behalf of the government, but members of the NDP point their finger at the member for Hamilton West. Indeed, I would be much disturbed if my remarks had gone unnoticed and unsung.
Clause 28 is what I call the Santa Claus clause. Under its provisions, if a person has been involved in the labour force for some 20 weeks, instead of paying him benefit on a week to week basis on the grounds of the amount of money that will be saved he will be paid three weeks benefit in advance. This is supposed to be an incentive to him to go out and find work. I stand here in utter amazement trying to rationalize this type of thinking. Just what are we attempting to do? No matter what the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) may think, I believe this would destroy personal initiative. It is a disincentive, and I have maintained this ever since I first saw the clause.
To use round figures, if a person is earning $150 a week he will be entitled to $100 unemployment insurance benefit. If he receives a total of $300 in unemployment insurance benefits all at once, is this an incentive for him to go out and look for a job? This is what the minister says. The vast majority of Canadians will do just that. Again, what disturbs me about this bill is that it is holding out inducements and I would not blame people if they took advantage of the legislation. But why do we attempt to create such a climate? The minister says that this provision will save money. Are we not concerned about the results, the implications, the ramifications of this attempt to save money? What are the equities?
The hon. member for Broadview seems to think that I have forgotten about the problems of the workingman. Mr. Speaker, I come from the great city of Hamilton which is presently celebrating its 125th anniversary. I don't stand here playing footsie. I am looking at both sides of the question. A lot of workers have told me they wonder just what is going on in connection with this Santa Clause clause. A lot of people involved with unem-
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
ployment insurance, workers who will be contributing, just do not understand the philosophy behind such a provision.
Mr. Speaker, I could add word upon word upon word. I
could be as repetitious as possible. Perhaps that is the problem with a debate such as this, that we continually repeat ourselves. But as long as we have legislation with clauses such as this, I personally would say to the Canadian people, "Go and take advantage of it. You are not breaking any law, but in taking advantage of it you are destroying your initiative and adopting a questionable philosophy".
I brought this motion before the House in order that we may bring some sanity back to the legislation. Certainly we are all interested in upgrading the Unemployment Insurance Act, certainly we all want higher benefits and reduced eligibility periods-but within reason. That is all we are talking about. So, Mr. Speaker, I end on a note of concern. I hope my remarks this evening will have some effect on this particular clause. I therefore take issue with clause 28.

Speaker, may I in my opening remarks use a word that my hon. friend from Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) used in his opening sentence. He said that he stood in his place amazed at this proposal. I stand in my place amazed at his opposition to it. Throughout this debate I have been puzzled by the way in which my friend and some of his colleagues at times seem to be on the side of the workers and at times against what I think are their best interests. I want to say categorically that I think the proposal in clause 28 is a good one. I commend the author of it, whoever he may be, the minister or even his parliamentary secretary or one of the bureaucrats upstairs. The minister is pointing upstairs, so the author can take a bow.
Let us look at a few of the details of this provision, Mr. Speaker. As the language indicates, it is a provision for paying in advance the first three weeks of an unemployment insurance benefit to which a claimant becomes entitled. In order to obtain that so-called advance payment the claimant in the first place must have gone through a two-week waiting period during which he received no benefit of any kind. If he has had a day's work in that period the amount he earns will be deducted from the advance of his unemployment insurance benefit. In addition to that, when he became unemployed it must have been because of a shortage of work. He cannot come under this program because he decided he was ill, and a female employee cannot come under it because of pregnancy. In addition, the employer must have certified that the lay-off will be for at least five weeks.

Far from this being a violation of the principles of insurance, and far from it being something based on the lowest instincts of human nature, I submit that this is a good thing. I think it is also true, as was demonstrated in committee, that it will simplify administration. Many of these cases will not have to be dealt with again. By the end of that period many persons will have found employment and will not have to return for three different payments. I think it makes administrative sense. My friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West, and I are supported by our seconders. I have the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) and the hon. member for Hamilton West has the hon. member for Moncton (Mr.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) wants to know which side we are on. I am prepared to support this amendment. The amendment would delete all of clause 28. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has properly said, if a person is unemployed, provided the employer certifies in accordance with paragraph (b) that "at the time of his interruption of earnings neither he nor his employer expected that he would be re-employed by that employer for a period of at least five weeks", he receives an advance of three weeks benefits provided he has been out of work for two weeks.
When asking which side we are on it is necessary to consider who is paying for this program. Somebody has said that it is the taxpayer. I will particularize. Unless the money comes out of the treasury it will come from contributions by the worker and the employer. No one will deny that ever since the act came into effect the rates have gone up from time to time. If this money comes out of the treasury it still comes from the taxpayer
June 10, 1971

who is either an employee or employer. It is the same class of people. I will particularize this clause in a minute. The money will come from the pocket of either the employee or the employer. If the fund runs out of money it must be replenished by money from the treasury, which actually comes out of the pocket of the taxpayer.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and his colleagues always leave the impression that they are the only ones who speak for the working man. This covers a broad section of the vote. The fact is that employees are contributing to the fund. If a man is out of work for two weeks and his employer has certified that he probably will not get work for five weeks, if he finds work two weeks and one day later he keeps the advance and his salary. He makes no contribution to the fund. My idea of insurance and the idea of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre certainly differ. With the greatest respect, I do not think this is insurance. I say that anyone who supports the amendment and opposes this clause is on the side of the worker.
Everywhere in this country workers have a fear about their security, particularly with this government. They are complaining that they have very little take-home pay compared to the amount they are earning. Clause 28 makes gifts; it does not matter how the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre dishes it up. I have faith in my fellow men. However, if a man receives and advance for three weeks and gets a job within two weeks and a day, and does not make any contribution to the fund, somebody has to make up that amount.
What is this all about? I hear the members of the NDP talking. I hear them hammer the government. Tonight the NDP and the government are in the same bed; they have married the same partner. I have heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre talk. I did not take part in many of the meetings of the committee. I certainly was not present when the arguments about this clause were presented. But I can tell the hon. member for Calgary North that when I first read the proposals in the bill this clause struck me as being one of the most realistic and helpful changes being proposed as far as many of the workers in my area are concerned.
We are faced with this situation: if a person works, having been unemployed for two weeks and one day, the most he stands to get as far as net income is concerned over and above what he has lost, is four days' pay. Even disregarding the fact that remuneration from the unemployment insurance fund will only amount to a percentage of his regular pay, a percentage of four days' pay
will be his net gain if he goes back to work after being unemployed for two weeks and one day. I urge the hon. member for Hamilton West and the hon. member for Calgary North to put this matter into perspective before they start talking as if this proposal would weaken the morale of the working force of Canada or add great new impetus to the rise in the cost of living, precipitate strikes, and so on.
This clause is not mandatory. The key word is "might". I suggest this applies to people who have established a fairly regular pattern of attachment to the labour force, usually over a period of years, people who are subject to only occasional, periodic interruption of regular employment. As soon as they return to work they begin to make contributions to the fund again. As a result of their pattern of work they will soon pay back the extra four days' pay they may have gained. They will pay it back out of their own contributions; they will not be leaning on the contributions of other workers.
In my view this arrangement may eliminate a great many headaches which occur in my constituency. The provisions may well apply to the whole group of loggers on the Pacific coast who regularly have what we call a fire season in the summer or a shutdown because of snow conditions in the winter. At times like these there are massive lay-offs of workers in a whole industry and there is not much alternative employment. This situation has created a great many difficulties as far as administration of the act is concerned and, hopefully, the change proposed will do much to remedy it. These are predictable lay-offs which create a situation where opportunities for alternative employment are, shall we say, virtually nonexistent for a short and rather specific period of time.
Perhaps the hon. member for Hamilton West will come to Vancouver Island some time during the nice, warm summer weather so that he can do a little fishing and also see what happens in the logging industry where workers are normally employed on a quite regular basis and are in a fairly well paid wage bracket, which meEins they make substantial contributions to the fund. I think he would come to appreciate the practicality of what this clause proposes, at least in respect of certain segments of the Canadian work force. This clause may be of no benefit to people who work in an industrial city like Hamilton; he may see it as a provision that will drain money from the pockets of workers in Hamilton to fill the pockets in some other parts of the country.
What I am trying to suggest to the hon. member, if he will examine the picture, is that the clause applies to the group of workers that I suggest can statistically be shown to be self-supporting and self-sustaining as far as their contributions to the fund are concerned. The way this clause will work, as I see it, is that it means there will be a lot less headaches for the workers as well as for the Unemployment Insurance Commission administratively; and within the established framework of a two-week waiting period it makes plain, good, ordinary common-sense to me to put this kind of clause in the bill.

June 10, 1971

I am trying to point out to the hon. member for Hamilton West that in considering the desirability of removing this clause from the bill he may have overlooked the real and practical situation that applies to some segments of the working force. At the present time there is a slackness in demand for pulp and paper products in the markets of the world. One of the pulp mills in my constituency has announced it is going to shut down for a period of five or six weeks. I would see this clause applying to the workers of that mill. It is possible that the workers of this mill may find an opening at another pulp mill that is not closing down, either within two weeks, after two weeks and one day, or after three weeks of unemployment. But such openings in the industry at other plants in the region are going to be few and far between.
I suggest that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is quite right in saying that if, under circumstances like these, those workers have an opportunity to get a job at another plant where their employment may be more regular than is the case at the plant where they have been working, they will take it. They will not stay unemployed for another week, if there is a chance of a job, simply to draw what is just a part of their normal income by collecting an extra three, or four or five days' unemployment insurance benefits.
Therefore, I hope the hon. member for Hamilton West will reconsider his position on this amendment. I think it is in contradiction with what I have come to feel is a general appreciation of the basic value of an unemployment insurance scheme.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this party have been accused more than once during this debate of being illog.cal and inconsistent. Without admitting that, I will say that it is very difficult to be consistent in this debate when we hear members to our left trying to justify all positions and using all sorts of arguments in support of those positions. This clause is a good example.
We were told during the committee hearings that the whole purpose of the three weeks' payment in advance is to provide an incentive to get people back to work. However, I have suspected right from the start that the main reason for this three-week period is that the department figures this is the easiest way out. There is less administrative cost involved if these people are paid three weeks' benefits than in trying to get them back to work.
Having listened to the members of the NDP this evening, my suspicions are confirmed. Both speakers who preceded me stated that once these people have got past the two-week period they will probably be unemployed for at least five weeks. In other words, they are admitting it is difficult to get these people back to work and therefore it is easier to pay them three weeks' benefits in order to get them off their hands.
The previous speaker talked about the situation in his area where it is difficult to get people back to work. In effect, what he said was that we should give these people 24107-674
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
three weeks' benefits and get them out of our hair for a while. As I say, I suspect this is tne real reason for this clause. Certainly it was indicated by the departmental officials that this would mean lower costs administratively. In that way they will only have to deal with these people once, or perhaps twice if the payment is split in half as has been suggested.
All through this debate we have been accused of lack of logic. I stated earlier this afternoon that the whole bill is illogical and has many inconsistencies. We are told that this provision was put in as a;i incentive to get people back to work, but as far as I am concerned, no one has yet justified that argument. What incentive is there for a man to go back to work if he is paid three weeks' benefits after he has been out of work for two weeks?

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speechtext: Certainly.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. member was listening to my illustration of a lay-off in the pulp and paper industry, but would he not agree with me that if a man has his three-week benefit cheque and he knows there is a chance of a job at another pulp mill that may be more permanent than his present job and which is 100 or 150 miles away, he is much more likely to look for a job at that mill with three weeks' pay in his pocket than sit around at home waiting for his next cheque to come along?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
That may or may not be the
case. On the other hand, a man who has settled in a community may not find the three weeks' payment sufficient inducement to travel 150 miles to get another job. But that is a specific case and I am not talking about specific cases. In some cases people may do that, but I think the main reason for this clause is that the department figures it is cheaper to handle the men in this way. This is where our friends to the left are not consistent. Far from being an incentive to a man to go back to work, this three weeks benefit is an incentive to stay at home.
Another thing that bothers me is the administrative nightmare that will result from this bill. I asked the officials about this matter in committee. I told them that as I understood it the only way a man could qualify for the three weeks' payment in advance was if he had a certificate of separation from his employer to the effect that he expected to be laid off more than five weeks. The officials agreed that I was correct, that in that case he would qualify for the three weeks' advance payment.
On the other hand, if an employer was perfectly honest and did not know how long the man in question would be laid off, and perhaps thought he might only be laid off three or four weeks, then after the second week, since the man did not have a certificate of separation that he expected to be laid off for more than five weeks, all he could receive from the fund is the weekly payment in. advance. Certainly he would not get the full three weeks.

June 10, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971
In this area I say the bill is an administrative nightmare. It places the onus on the employer to estimate the period of lay-off. This can be done by a large corporation like General Motors where there may be a lay-off for six or eight weeks, but I suggest the small employer cannot do this.
It was very illuminating to me to hear what one of the hon. members to the left had to say about a question I asked in committee. This shows that hon. members to the left try to justify ah positions. I asked the officials whether this provision would not place too much onus on the employer and create a great deal of dissatisfaction. It was interesting to hear the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) say that then the employee will probably try to seduce the employer into giving him a separation certificate. These hon. gentlemen point accusingly at us and say we suspect that all men are dishonest. Apparently these thoughts run through their minds. Why would that member of the NDP make such a statement as this, because it could lead to collusion between employer and the employee.
I point this out as another example of the nightmare this measure will create. If on the one hand the employer says he has left for four weeks, he gets no payment; if the employer gives him a certificate for five weeks or more, he is immediately handed a three-week payment in advance. If this is an incentive for a man to go back to work, I am very badly mistaken. I strongly support this amendment because I feel the whole purpose of the clause is to take the onus off the department, by allowing it to say to these people, "You can have three weeks' payment, but don't come back for three weeks; we do not intend to find you a job."

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the minister in connection with one or two points referred to in the remarks of the previous speaker. I realize that most Canadians are honest, but the thought has occurred to me after reading the clause that a racket might be worked out through collusion between a crooked employee and a sleight-of-hand employer. Having made that observation, what provision or restraint has the department thought of in order to avoid a situation such as that taking place? I am not suggesting for a moment that anyone would do this, but after all there are 21 million people in this country and I have reason to believe that some of them are not as full of integrity as they should be. While I am not of a suspicious nature, it seems to me there is here a beautiful loophole for a dandy racket. I would ask the minister to explain the safeguards against such a possibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT, COMMISSION, BENEFITS, PREMIUMS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would much prefer to deal with that question when we reach the clause of the bill that provides penalties and regulations. I will not forget to deal with it then. Quite properly, the hon. member has pointed out that there is a possibility and a danger here of collusion between a dishonest employer and a dishonest employee. This is true of any part of the act; it is not restricted to this part. If you have a dishon-
[Mr. Thomas (Moncton) .1
est employee and a dishonest employer in this combination, this could exist because it is human nature. We have ways and means of dealing with it.
When we get to that part of the bill dealing with the fines and court action available to the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the procedure to eliminate this type of abuse, I will deal with it. I will point out the legal action that can be taken against such a dishonest employer and employee. I think you will find that the fines and penalties provided therein are more than ample in the way of deterrent to prevent any such widespread fraud, because that is what it would be in the case that has been presented. When we reach that point I will deal much more specifically with the question.
I might say while I am on my feet that the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas) made a very valid point. It would be wrong and dishonest on my part to deny that administratively this tidies up or makes the role of the Unemployment Insurance Commission much easier. I think this is the point that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) mentioned. If a person is unemployed, the commission will ascertain whether he can take advantage of this feature, or to whom this clause of the act applies. There are people, for instance, who are unemployed as a result of sickness or maternity and who therefore are not eligible for advance payment. This advance payment does not apply to anybody other than those with the proper period of attachment.
If an employer believes that his employee will be without work for at least five weeks, then a certificate is issued. In that case, if the person happens to be unemployed in a region that is very badly affected by unemployment- and the hon. member for Moncton has quite realistically suggested that the chances of his getting back to work are not good,-then the chances are he will be unemployed for the five-week period, in which case this provision makes sound sense administratively.
The hon. member made quite a good case for keeping this clause in, having regard to the administrative feature. He suggested it will save a considerable sum of money in respect of unemployment insurance. We cannot have it both ways. If we want an administratively good plan, and if this is going to save money, we should not remove a clause which accord ng to the hon. member for Moncton would make it possible for the administrators of the plan to save that money. I think this clause should be supported for that reason, in addition to the valid reason suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member from British Columbia regarding the incentive features of the plan.
I think the hon. member from Moncton quite properly pointed out that the three weeks' advance payment will be paid in two payments. Quite frankly, the reason for this is that in long periods of unemployment we felt that the time between the first cheque and the next would be about four weeks and this would mean no income for a month. This is essentially the basic reason for dividing the three-week payment into two cheques.

Dealing with the first part of the question, in the circumstances outlined by the hon. member this would not preclude an employer from hiring the same employee. I was answering a specific case of collusion described by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. McCutcheon). He referred to a situation involving a dishonest employer and a dishonest employee. That is the case I referred to when pointing out that there are penalties in the act to protect the Canadian public and the fund against this kind of combination of a dishonest employer and a dishonest employee.
In so far as the second question is concerned, I am sure there will be cases where an employer has filed a certificate stating that an employee, according to the act, will be unemployed for five weeks. He might subsequently find himself in the happy position, both for himself and his employee, of being able to bring the man back to work sooner than anticipated because of unexpected circumstances. It is not our intention in that case to deal with the employee any differently than if the employer had hired someone other than his normal employee.
To answer the second part of the question, may I say that in those rare occasions when an employer certifies that an employee will not be rehired, and there is a change and the employee is rehired, in that five-week period he is still entitled to assistance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking in this adjournment debate perhaps I should first inquire whether either the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) or his parliamentary secretary are prepared to answer this question. I do not see either of these gentleman in the House. It would be useless to put the question in some detail unless someone is prepared to answer for the Minister of Transport. It is obviously a vital question for Prince Edward Island. Perhaps the fact that neither the minister nor his parliamentary secretary saw fit to be here is a further reflection of the growing lack of concern and interest in the transportation problems of Prince Edward Island.
It was on June 2 that questions were put in the House during the question period with respect to the increase in ferry rates both to the province of P.E.I. and to Newfoundland. The rate increases with respect to P.E.I. were in the range of from 50 per cent to 100 per cent and, as in so many things in recent years, there was no forewarning that such action would be taken, even though this action was taken without any obvious consultation with the government of P.E.I. I should hasten to add that if there was any consultation in advance, certainly no evidence of it was forthcoming from either the Premier or the Minister of Tourism.
Second, it becomes apparent that there was very little forewarning to those who operate the ferry service. I think that that again must be considered to be an example of an unilateral decision that is taken without adequate consultation and without adequate concern for the needs and the rights of the people of P.E.I. It is the smallest province but surely these people deserve the same kind of consideration that people in other parts of this country have a right to expect.
In a general way, since this government took office three years ago there has been a continuing decline in interest on the part of the government in the transportation problems of P.E.I. It began first with a callous disre-

maintopic: TRANSPORT-REVIEW BY GOVERNMENT OF FERRY RATE INCREASES IMPOSED BY CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS IN MARITIMES
speechtext:
Again, recently this year we saw another unilateral decision taken to remove the flagship of the line, the John Hamilton Grey, for a portion of the year from the P.E.I. service. Again there was no consultation, forewarning or indication that this ship, which had been christened with the names of two Fathers of Confederation from New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, would be so cavalierly removed from its basic area of service.
In its place, two summer ferries have been added. Having travelled on these ferries I can say that in terms of transportation they are adequate if not luxrious, but they have particular faults which I think bring great dangers to the federal government. If the minister had been here this evening I would have pointed out the great danger to life which exists in the staircase and fire doors that have been installed in these ferries which make them literally unsafe for persons travelling. I should like to ask the minister at some point what steps he plans to take to deal with the various lawsuits that I am sure he will encounter from people who are more than likely to suffer grievous accident because of these inadequately installed staircases.
I want to deal specifically this evening with the rate increases because it is in this area that most recently the people of P.E.I. are aware of the government's lack of concern, the lack of willingness to consult with the elected authorities of the province, the lack of willingness to state the reasons for which the increases are necessary, and the lack of willingness to state why the subsidy in the case of Northumberland Ferries was to be decreased by a substantial sum, close to $200,000, and that these rates would go into effect at very short notice before anyone has had a chance to ascertain their effect with regard to the second most important industry in P.E.I., namely, the tourist industry.
The minister is not here this evening and neither is his parliamentary secretary. Again, it seems that we are going to be served up with some kind of formalized answer with respect to transportation, which is a binding part of the commitment between this country and the province of Prince Edward Island, entered into at the time of confederation. I think it is a sorry fact that during the last three years we have seen the transportation needs of the province of P.E.I. downgraded and the erosion of decades of progress made in improving transportation to the province. It is about time the minister and the government treated seriously both the long-term and short-term transportation requirements of that province.
Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance': Mr. Speaker, in the unavoidable absence
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Duquet) I have the honour of replying to the hon. member on behalf of the minister. I would like to provide some information relevant to the question of passenger ferry rates which now are in existence on the east coast and to which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) announced changes on Tuesday.
I am sure the hon. member is familiar with the changes to these rates announced by the minister which affect ferry services under Department of Transport jurisdiction, namely, the Gulf Service to Newfoundland and the Borden-Tormentine service. As a result of the minister's intervention the rates which were originally introduced for the summer ferry services were substantially reduced. I should like to read from the very brief public statement which was made by the Minister of Transport on Tuesday, affecting the Borden-Tormentine service:
In view of representations I received today upon my return to Ottawa I have instructed that the proposed summer rates not be introduced on the Borden-Tormentine ferry service. This means that the new winter rates will apply year round. These involve an increase per passenger of only 15 cents, with no increase for children, and an extra 50 cents only for automobiles. The rate for trailers will increase by just 5 cents per foot with no change in the present minimum.
In addition to this, the minister indicated that he had spoken to the president of the Canadian Transport Commission regarding the Wood Islands-Caribou service. Late Tuesday the water transport committee of the CTC accepted an application from Northumberland Ferries Limited to cancel the new summer rate schedule for that service and to revert to the winter rates announced June 7. While these rates are higher than in other years, they are considerably less than the summer rates which were announced.
I believe the hon. member is aware that there has been little change to ferry rate schedules on the east coast for many years-in one service I believe it was 1949, and in another 1955. Over that period of time the cost of maintaining the service has been increasing steadily. In the past few years considerable expenditures have been made by the federal government in order to provide our two island provinces with fast, comfortable and efficient ferry service. There is no doubt that tourists and the travelling public, while they will be paying a little more for transportation to and from the islands will be getting a better quality of service than has ever before existed in terms of accommodation, frequency and speedier vessels.
The minister's announcement on Tuesday has been understood and appreciated in the Atlantic area. The hon. member has made a number of points which I have not covered since there was no indication in the original question that they would be raised. I will certainly bring these to the attention of the minister.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, June 7, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) whether the House could expect a statement from a member of the government following the meeting of the NATO council at Lisbon. Considering that the Lisbon meeting concluded on the preceding Friday, I thought it incumbent upon some member of the government to make a statement thereon. I state this noting that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), who spends a great deal of time abroad, had not deigned to return to Ottawa before leaving for a Washington ministerial meeting where, incidentally, he failed to discuss the TAPS project despite undertakings given previously. I may also say that I am not disturbed by the Prime Minister's posture of condescending indifference, having grown accustomed to it. However, I find it something less than a proper attitude to adopt to an inquiry on a matter so important as a top-level meeting of NATO.
It has been a fairly well-developed pattern in this country that ministers returning from NATO gatherings would report to Parliament and to the country on the main lines of deliberation in this alliance of which Canada is a charter member and was once a very important participant. Perhaps it is the intention of the present government to downplay and denigrate the NATO alliance and Canada's membership therein. From some recent actions and many utterances we might well be inclined to believe that this is the case.
Perhaps this glibness on the part of the Prime Minister merely reinforces a growing opinion in this country that it is a part of the present government's intention to downplay, denigrate and diminish the importance of Canada's role in this organization which has long been regarded as a bulwark of western defence, a buttress of western freedom and a meeting place wherein leaders of friendly nations could consolidate their positions and advance the interests of peace, prosperity and stability in a much broader way.
In recent weeks the foreign policy of the Canadian government has received severe strictures from many Canadians who fear that their Prime Minister is leading them into policy paths which do not reflect this country's aims and interests. It strikes me that the Prime Minister, in the face of widespread misunderstanding of his Russian visit, would seize an early opportunity to clarify the role of Canada in NATO. The fact that this occasion was not used but that the Prime Minister showed his usual impolite cynicism on the matter aggravates rather than ameliorates, the feelings of many alert and thoughtful Canadians whom he is supposed to lead in the realms of foreign policy.
I hope that whoever speaks on behalf of the Prime Minister will be able to explain this seeming lack of interest in the NATO meeting and will tell us why so scant attention is paid to this top-level meeting in Lisbon. Perhaps we will be told, also, if and when the Parliament
of Canada, representing the people of Canada, may hear a report on the actions and utterances of government representatives in the meetings of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization recently concluded.

speakeroldname: Mr. Barnett J. Danson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: TRANSPORT-REVIEW BY GOVERNMENT OF FERRY RATE INCREASES IMPOSED BY CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS IN MARITIMES
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON NATO FOREIGN MINISTERS MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not realize that this occasion was to be used for a diatribe against the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) nor to suggest a further downgrading of Parliament by not permitting the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) to reply and report to Parliament on his attendance at the NATO meeting in Lisbon.
As the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) knows, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is attending meetings in Washington on very important environmental problems. He will be returning to the House on Monday, when he will make a complete statement to the House on motions. I think, Mr. Speaker, that is the reply that this Parliament deserves and which it will get.
I am surprised that the hon. member for Hillsborough has used the occasion to also suggest that the foreign policy initiatives which this government has taken, particularly in relation to the recent visit to the Soviet Union, are not reflecting the views of the Canadian people. Certainly they reflect leadership on the part of the government, leadership that I think is well accepted and understood by the Canadian people. Perhaps they are not understood by the opposition but I think the people of Canada look with the same hope as this government to the outcome of the recent initiatives with the Soviet Union.
To answer the specific question, the Secretary of State for External Affairs will be in the House on Monday on his return from this very important meeting in Washington, and will report fully to Parliament as is the practice.

subsubtopic: HOUSING-THE RICHMOND SQUARE APARTMENT PROJECT, TORONTO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this matter concerns the potentially tragic situation created by the sinking of the CMHC financed Richmond Square (Limited Dividend) apartment housing project in my riding of Spadina, in Toronto. This project covers half a city block on the north side of Richmond Street West between Niagara Street and Walnut Avenue. It backs on a lane at the rear of stores and service stations on the south side of Queen Street West. I understand that the whole project was designed to contain 545 suites, the majority of which are likely contained in the 13-storey high-rise building that is now posing the menace of this collapse.
My information is that a private contractor agreed to build this project as a low-rental housing project under the terms of the National Housing Act, by which the builder's profits are limited. If this information is incorrect, the minister is here this evening to correct it. I do not know whether the mortgage loan for this project from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is an 85 per cent or 95 per cent mortgage. I would be interested in
[Mr. Deputy Speaker.)
June 10, 1971

knowing the exact situation. I have not seen the application or the terms of agreement between the parties, nor do I know how many thousands or millions of dollars have been advanced under the CMHC commitment to this private builder.
I do know that the building permit was obtained last fall, that despite the usual soil testing, the footings were improperly placed and in any event were probably inadequate. There should likely have been a reinforced concrete pad under at least part of the substructure. Such footings or sills were built lengthwise with the bed of a former creek and have failed to support the structure. I say this because the 13-storey, multimillion dollar part of this project has sunk into the ground and every floor has a sag in it. Local people say that this is symbolic of the Trudeau depression.
I am advised that the interior of the building was finished during the winter and one can see from the outside that the interior painting appears to have been completed. The floors, ceilings and bearing walls have obviously settled and are perhaps 10 to 20 inches out of line. There are approximately 80 apartments in which the windows have popped in or out.
I am advised by an official of the city of Toronto that as the building went up and the frost came out of the ground this spring, a large portion of the building subsided. Apparently the building should have been tenanted long before this but no one who sees the obvious fault in construction wants to move in. Even to a layman's eye the sag in the building poses a hazard to the unaffected parts of the building, adjacent buildings and passing traffic. The sag is obvious on both the north and south sides of the building and in the garage area underneath, where some attempt has apparently been made to support or raise the footings that have sunk. It may be that this building will stand for some while without further settlement, but obviously it will continue to be a menace and with the return of frost in the ground next winter it may be weakened further.
It is imperative that the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras) responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation look into this matter forthwith. I am sure he will. I think that the building should be condemned and demolished either in whole or in part. There is no question but that the 80 units are and will continue to be a dead loss. Expert engineering advice is needed, and reassessment of the whole project. In view of this grossly negligent, if not criminally negligent chance taken with people's lives and public money, the Minister without Portfolio's supervision of CMHC comes seriously into question.
Section 13 (3) of the National Housing Act reads:
No contract shall be entered into with a builder unless
(A)	The project is completed and is built in an area satisfactory to the corporation and in accordance with standards of construction approved by the corporation and
(B)	The project consists of 8 or more family housing units and is designed to provide housing accommodation of a size and type prescribed by the corporation.

In addition, there is the duty of thorough inspection by CMHC officials. In this they have failed. In their inspections and approvals they are not using good methods and good judgment. The tragedy of St. Jean Vianney is another example of poor judgment and inefficiency in this corporation. It was a CMHC-built subdivision that was involved in that landslide. If many more of these cases of negligent engineering, negligent inspection and poor selection of sites come to light-and according to present experience they well might-the corporation's Mortgage Insurance Fund and will be as bankrupt as this government is of competence.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan) is unusually full of fire and brimstone tonight. From the information I have been able to gather since he raised this question this morning, I cannot recogn'ze the project he is describing as being the same one that goes under the name of Richmond Square. This is a project for which a loan was approved in July of 1970 in the amount of $2,300,000 for a project under section 16, comprising 228 housing units-not 500, the number he mentioned-to be built on Niagara Street in Toronto. This is known as Richmond Square. So I think we are pretty close to talking about the same project.

If there are any errors in this reply, and there may be some in the hon. member's presentation, we will investigate further. But to bring the matter up to date, as I think the hon. member knows these units were designed under section 16 for families of low and moderate incomes. The plans and drawing of the proposed building had the endorsation of consulting engineers and inspecting and testing engineers. Construction commenced in mid-April of last year and proceeded through the winter. By April 2 the construction was reported as being 60 per cent completed. On or about April 16 it was reported that settlement had taken place along one line of caissons. The city of Toronto immediately placed a stop order on the project and independent consulting engineers were brought in. These engineers ordered the building to be shored. This has now been done and the construction of the building is being proceeded with.
To date, CHMC has advanced $949,000 and, depending on engineering reports to be obtained, it looks as though the corporation will continue its advances as the project nears completion. That is the information I have at this stage. I will further investigate the matter raised and if there is any deviation from the information I have just given I will report it to the hon. member.
